utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We are now at the point of commencing the trial of the three accused, each of whom have previously entered pleas of not guilty to all counts in the indictment. The proceedings this morning have ensured that the present interpretation arrangements are adequate to ensure that each of the accused is able to follow the proceedings in their own language. So on that basis, we now turn to Mr. Cayley and invite him to make his opening remarks.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: May it please Your Honours. A few prefatory comments, Your Honours. I will be displaying during my opening a number of exhibits in the Sanction software system, so you'll see the document on the screen in front of you. All of the material has been disclosed to the Defence, although, of course, it will be admitted through later witnesses. A number of the documents are in fact public documents which will probably not require formal admission through a witness such as Security Council resolutions, public statements by the Prosecutor. So with that, Your Honours, I will begin.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The essential facts of this case are as straightforward as they are compelling. The Prosecutor will show that between May and July of 1998, Serb and Albanian men were abducted and unlawfully detained in a makeshift prison camp in the village of Lapusnik in Kosovo. Here, they were brutally beaten, tortured, and mistreated, and in over 20 instances, either beaten to death or killed by fatal gunshot wound. The three accused before you, Fatmir Limaj, Isak Musliu, and Haradin Bala, bear responsibility for these events. The origins of this case and the human suffering which both preceded and followed it are now part of European history. The hopes, frustrations, and irreconcilable differences which led to this war, while relevant for your consideration, are not on trial here. In bringing this case, we do not seek to underwrite or condemn the ethics or wisdom of any party who sought recourse to war as a means of settling bitter and seemingly intractable controversies. The causes of war, the aspirations of an oppressed people are not the subject of a complaint. The Prosecutor's position is simply this: No cause, however just, legitimises indiscriminate murder. The Prosecutor strived for the best part of ten years towards one straightforward objective: To condemn dispassionately, impartially, very serious crimes committed by any party which fall within the jurisdiction of this Tribunal. I hope you can see a map in front of you of where Kosovo lies in the Balkans. The beige shaded area is Kosovo. The crimes which are referred to in this indictment took place in Kosovo. You can see that Kosovo is located in the southern part of what was the former Yugoslavia. It shares borders with Montenegro to the west, Albania to the south-west, the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia to the south, and you can see Serbia to the north. The village of Lapusnik, which is the principal scene of the crimes in this indictment, you can see marked on this map. It is in the municipality of Glogovac. So you see it marked there with a red disk. Do Your Honours see the maps in front -- you do. Thank you. The village of Lapusnik is strategically located on the Pristina-Peja-Pec road. You can see there Pristina on the right. The cursor arrow is marking it. That is the major city, major capital of Pristina -- of Kosovo, rather, and then you can see to the left, Peja, or Pec as it is known in the Serbian language, which is another principal town in Kosovo. So Lapusnik is strategically located on a road connecting these two major places. By February or March of 1998, Kosovo had spiralled into armed conflict with the Serb army and police on one side and the KLA, or Kosovo Liberation Army, on the other. By May of 1998, Fatmir Limaj had returned from Switzerland and was based at the KLA headquarters in Klecka. He was commander of the KLA forces in an area where the crimes which are specified in this indictment took place. If we could now advance to the next exhibit. There you can see Klecka marked on the map. The cursor arrow is showing it. And you see Lapusnik, the principal scene of the crimes in the case, with the red square. Fatmir Limaj was the commander of KLA forces in an area where the crimes which are specified in the indictment took place. A number of KLA military concentrations or points, as they were called, were dispersed across Fatmir Limaj's area of control, including one in the village of Lapusnik. Again, the cursor pointing to the village of Lapusnik. Isak Musliu was commander of KLA troops in Lapusnik. The commanders or leaders of all of these points, including Isak Musliu, reported to Fatmir Limaj, and he, in turn, was regularly present at these points or military concentrations supervising and commanding his troops in the region. As part of an effort to strengthen his grip in his area of command, Fatmir Limaj and others, including Isak Musliu and Haradin Bala, participated in a campaign to target Serbs and Albanians accused of collaboration with the Serbs, with abduction, unlawful imprisonment, torture, and murder. Serbs, it seems, were arrested simply for being Serbs; Albanians, because of alleged collaboration. Often, it seems that collaboration was based on merely having had social contact with Serbs. Sometimes political loyalties at odds with the KLA political beliefs were the motivation. The evidence will show, Your Honours, that many more Albanians than Serbs were captured and taken to Lapusnik. Serbs and Albanians were abducted by members of the KLA from their homes, often in the middle of the night, often from public transport or their motor cars. They were taken from villages in Limaj's areas of command and brought, all of them, to the camp at Lapusnik. If Limaj's headquarters at Klecka did not order the kidnapping or know of it beforehand, they were informed immediately after it happened. Although many prisoners were interrogated, usually while being beaten, it was no effort to determine if there was any legal basis to detain them. Isak Musliu, as part of his command duties, was in charge of the soldiers who guarded the camp at Lapusnik. Haradin Bala was a guard in the camp. Both knew of and participated in atrocious criminal acts in the camp. Prisoners were kept in inhumane conditions. They were beaten and tortured. A number of prisoners were beaten to death in the camp or executed. Isak Musliu and Haradin Bala were based in Lapusnik and were regularly at the camp. Fatmir Limaj visited Lapusnik at least 20 times between May and July of 1998. He knew what was taking place in the makeshift camp and Isak Musliu acted to his order. The camp was in operation from May until July 26th, 1998, when a Serb counter-offensive in the region forced an evacuation of the remaining prisoners from the camp, who were taken up into the hills above Lapusnik to a place called Berisa. And you can see Berisa marked on the map with an orange triangle with a black circle within it. Here, on Fatmir Limaj's orders, approximately half of the remaining prisoners were released and the other half were executed by Haradin Bala. Those, Your Honours, are the essential facts of this case. Kosovo is currently supervised by a United Nations civilian interim administration. UNMIK, as it is known, the UN mission in Kosovo, was established by Security Council resolution in 1999, Resolution 1244, after the end of the war. This administration works closely with Kosovo's leaders and its people. The United Nations receives substantial support for its work in Kosovo from the organisation for security and cooperation in Europe, OSCE, and from the EU, from the European Union. KFOR, or Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond Kosovo Force is a NATO-led military force responsible for maintaining the peace and security in the region. I mentioned this to you because these acronyms I think you will hear throughout the trial. I'm quite certain you knew this already but I wanted to make it clear. Just a word on Albanian and Serbian or B/C/S as we call it at ICTY. You've already noticed on the maps that there are often times two names for the same place. In Kosovo, places obviously have names in the Albanian language and names in the Serbian language. The history of the region explains this. Obviously, Albanian witnesses will refer to place-names by their Albanian names, and Serb witnesses by their Serb names. Often times, the word is very similar or almost identical, but we will all I think become accustomed over the course of the trial with the fact that often times a single place may be referred to by two slightly different names. A word about the investigation of this case. A survivor, who you will hear as a witness, first made complaint to local police in Kosovo and then to the international police arm of UNMIK, the United Nations mission in Kosovo. It was UNMIK, or the international police arm of UNMIK, who commenced the first large-scale investigation of these crimes. The Prosecutor of the ICTY exercised her jurisdiction in this case in 2002, and the case was taken over at that time by the Office of the Prosecutor. I mention this, as you will see from time to time in the case witness statements and other material whose origin does not lie with this office but in fact with UNMIK. I should emphasise that the OTP re-investigated this case. By this I mean we spoke to all of the witnesses, or almost all of the witnesses who UNMIK identified in their investigation and then we obviously identified many more witnesses of our own. The Defence have all the material from the UNMIK investigation, which we required to disclose to them under the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, be that Rule 66 or Rule 68. The original UNMIK investigation targeted four individuals. We did the same. The three accused before you and another individual by the name of Agim Murtezi. Agim Murtezi was charged and arrested and claimed from the very start that he had been misidentified. None of the three other accused before you made such a claim. On transfer to The Hague, Murtezi immediately submitted to a suspect interview in accordance with the Rules with the Prosecutor. All of the other three accused exercised their legal right to remain silent. After further investigation of Murtezi's account by the Prosecutor, it was clear that he had not been in Lapusnik during the relevant time. Period he was released and the charges were dropped. One last word on UNMIK and KFOR. Our own investigation and work in Kosovo would not have been possible without the cooperation that we receive from these two organisations. People are working very hard, both internationals and senior members of both communities, to re-establish the rule of law and ensure that Kosovo has a transparent and functioning legal system. I publicly pay tribute and thank all of these individuals. In front of you, Your Honours, you will see a photograph of some housing and agricultural premises. Here you see a traditional Albanian compound. And where you see the cursor at the moment is the place in which the makeshift prison camp was established from May until July of 1998. Here you see a road where the cursor is now pointing, and above the road, another compound opposite the prison camp which served as a KLA headquarters. So it is in this area here, in these buildings surrounding where the arrow is pointing now, where the makeshift prison camp was located. Whilst not all the crimes contained in the indictment took place in the camp, it is here that victims were taken after their abduction. It is here where all of the victims in this case were unlawfully imprisoned. It is here where the victims were beaten, tortured, and maltreated, and it is either in this place or from here where the murder victims were taken to be killed. An opening statement must contain an outline of the evidence on which the Prosecutor intends to rely and also an explanation of the nature of the charges laid. The Prosecutor has already outlined the law and evidence in some detail in written form in her pre-trial brief. The three accused have all responded to that pre-trial brief in their own pre-trial briefs in which they outline their challenges to the Prosecutor's case and set out generally the nature of their defences to the allegations made against them. Some preliminary comments on the pre-trial briefs of the Defence, which respectfully, Your Honours, I would ask you to keep at the forefront of your mind throughout this opening and indeed throughout this case. The accused Limaj and Musliu acknowledge their presence in the village of Lapusnik for either virtually all or a substantial period of the indictment. Fatmir Limaj states that he was in Lapusnik on some 20 occasions between May and July of 1998. Isak Musliu states in his pre-trial brief that he was based in Lapusnik from May to July of 1998, although he took some trips away from Lapusnik at that time. Whilst admitting their presence in the very place where all of this suffering and killing took place, for those two accused, there was no camp, no prisoners, no beatings, no torture, and no dead that burdened their conscience. As is their right, the accused are putting the Prosecutor to proof on all the criminality referred to in this indictment. The Prosecutor will do exactly what is implicitly asked of her: Show to this Court their guilt beyond a reasonable doubt. Mr. Bala has taken a slightly different course in his defence than his co-accused. He offers to the Court a partial alibi. He states now that he was in Lapusnik for a few weeks in May of 1998, and then left for duties elsewhere. So his position is that he knew nothing about the camp either, although in the recently filed Rule 92 bis response by the Defence, it now seems that his position too is that he denies the existence of the prison camp also. So not only that he didn't know about it but that he completely denies that the camp ever existed. The principal strength of the Prosecutor's case, Your Honours, is that the Prosecutor draws on evidence from multiple sources. We do not just call the victims, the survivors, we also rely on forensic evidence, which is unusual for a war crimes case because of the length of time normally between commission and length of trial. Moreover, the evidence of the survivors is corroborated by members of the international community, who will confirm that during the relevant time period, it was well known that both Serbs and Albanians were being abducted and murdered by certain elements within the KLA. We will rely on evidence from members of the KLA itself, individuals who were on the inside of the organisation, who will confirm, either partly or fully, a number of the critical events in this case. If I could now make some comments, Your Honours, about the indictment structure and the charges, quite briefly. All three accused are charged with unlawful imprisonment in count 1 as a crime against humanity and count 2 as a violation of the laws or customs of war. Fatmir Limaj and Isak Musliu are charged under Article 7(1) and 7(3) of the Statute with these crimes, Haradin Bala is charged under Article 7(1) only. All three accused are charged with torture, inhumane acts and cruel treatment. Torture is charged in counts 3 and 4 as a crime against humanity and a violation of the laws and customs of war respectively; inhumane acts are charged as a violation of the laws and customs of war in count 5; and cruel treatment is charged in count 6, again as a violation of the laws and customs of war. In respect of these counts, Fatmir Limaj and Isak Musliu are charged under Article 7(1) and 7(3) of the Statute, Haradin Bala is charged under Article 7(1) only. All three accused are charged with murder. Murder is charged in count 7 as a crime against humanity, and in count 8 as a violation of the laws and customs of war. These counts capture the murder of Ajet Gashi, the murder of Milovan Krstic, the murder of Miodrag Krstic, the murder of Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond Slobodan Mitrovic, the murder of Miroslav Suljnic, the murder of Zivorad Krstic, the murder of Stamen Genov, the murder of Djordje Cuk, the murder of Sinisa Blagojevic, the murder of Jefta Petkovic, the murder of Zvonko Marinkovic, the murder of Agim Ademi and the murder of Vesel Ahmeti and the murder of Fehmi Xhema. Fatmir Limaj and Isak Musliu are charged with the unlawful killing of these men under both Article 7(1) and 7(3) of the Statute. Haradin Bala is charged under Article 7(1) only of the Statute, with the murder of Jefta Petkovic, Zvonko Marinkovic, Agim Ademi, Vesel Ahmeti and Fehmi Xhema. Murder is charged in counts 9 and 10 as a crime against humanity and violation of the laws and customs of war. These two counts capture the murder of Emin Emini, the murder of Ibush Hamza, the murder of Hyzri Harjizi, the murder of Shaban Hoti, the murder of Hasan Hoxha, the murder of Safet Hysenaj, the murder of Bashkim Rashiti, the murder of Hetem Rexhaj, the murder of Lutfi Xhemshiti, and the murder of Shyqyri Zymeri. Fatmir Limaj is charged with all of these murders under both Article 7(1) and 7(3) of the Statute. Haradin Bala is charged with these murders under Article 7(1) only. A brief word on the modes of liability on which we rely under Article 7(1) of the Statute. You will see in the indictment in the prefatory paragraphs for each series of counts - that's paragraphs 21, 25, 28, and 34 - that these express the modes of liability that we rely on for that particular set of counts, where Fatmir Limaj and Isak Musliu are charged under Article 7(1) of the Statute, the modes we rely on are planning, instigating, ordering, committing, or otherwise aiding and abetting. Where Haradin Bala is charged under Article 7(1) of the Statute, we rely only on the modes of committing or otherwise aiding and abetting. Where we state the mode of liability of committing, we seek to plead, where appropriate, that not only did the accused personally participate in the alleged crime, where the evidence so demonstrates, but also that these crimes were part of a joint criminal enterprise in which all three accused participated. We've expressly pleaded the nature of that joint criminal enterprise in paragraphs 6 to 13 of the indictment. You will recall that the Tadic appeals judgement identified three forms of joint criminal enterprise, and I will deal with those three forms at a later stage in my opening. At this juncture, I would simply say this about the legal vehicle of liability of joint criminal enterprise: In a joint criminal enterprise, we do not seek to punish one man for another man's crimes. We seek to punish each for his own crime of joining a common criminal plan in which others also participated. The measure of the criminality of the plan and therefore of the guilt of each participant is of course the sum total of all the crimes committed by all in executing the plan. But the basis of the offence is participation in the formulation and/or execution of the plan. These are the rules which every civilised society has found necessary in order to reach men who do not always get blood on their own hands but who lay plans or involve themselves in a plan that result in the shedding of blood. What will become clear from the evidence is that the abduction, imprisonment, maltreatment and murder of the victims in this case was a criminal enterprise of some scale and longevity. Whilst it is true that the three accused are not the only ones involved in these --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please slow down for the interpreters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm running ahead of the translators. What I will do is to turn up the French translation and listen to it here and hopefully that should solve it. So all three accused are charged under Article 7(1) with criminal responsibility for their participation in a joint criminal enterprise. Who are the three accused? Firstly, the first accused, Fatmir Limaj. The first accused is 33 years old. He was born in Banja near Malisevo, in Kosovo, and you can see Banja. The cursor is pointing to the village of Banja now. You can also see still identified Lapusnik above it. So Mr. Limaj was a local man from this area. He served as deputy defence minister in the provisional government of Kosovo and was later a member of the Pristina Municipal Assembly and was the PDK public relations secretary. The PDK, or Kosovo Democratic Party, is a party which emerged from the renamed PPDK, which was a political party that emerged out of the KLA. Mr. Limaj was educated in Kosovo and studied law at the University of Pristina. He was active from a young age in resisting Serb rule in Kosovo. He joined the KLA prior to the war in 1998, after a crack-down by Serb authorities against Kosovar Albanian organisations. He sought refugee status in Switzerland in 1997. Here he stayed until about March of 1998, when he returned to Kosovo and established a KLA headquarters in Klecka, the place that I've already shown to you on the map. You can see it again on this map - the white cursor is pointing to it - where he controlled KLA forces south of the strategic Pristina-Pec road, which is this road here. By May of 1998, forces under Fatmir Limaj's control had secured the village of Lapusnik, which then served as a front line base for both KLA operations against the Serbs and as the prison camp for Serb and Albanian prisoners. From at least this time, Limaj went under the pseudonym or nom de guerre of Celiku, and the unit under his command at Lapusnik which was commanded by the second accused in this case, Isak Musliu, was known as Celiku 3. The second accused, Isak Musliu. Isak Musliu is also 33 years old. He was born in the village of Racak. You can see Racak there marked on the map. Also a local man. He completed military service with the JNA in 1989. He joined the KLA in 1996, and in April of 2000, he joined the KPS or Kosovo Police Service. He was dismissed from the police on the 9th of May, 2002. His nom de guerre during the war was Qerqiz. Shortly after the 9th of May of 1998, Musliu became the commander of KLA soldiers in Lapusnik directly under Fatmir Limaj. He was the local commander of forces in Lapusnik as opposed to Fatmir Limaj, who was the regional commander. Isak Musliu's role was to organise part of the defence of the Lapusnik area and command the guards that ran the camp. The third accused in this case, Mr. Haradin Bala, was born in Korotice E Eperme, and you can see that also where the cursor is now pointing, also a local man. He has a heart condition for which he's currently being successfully treated, and whilst he has argued that such condition makes him unfit to stand trial before you, physicians have concluded that he is currently fit to be with us. Haradin Bala joined the KLA in April 1998. He went to Lapusnik in May of 1998. He was a guard at the Lapusnik prison camp. From this time, he went under the pseudonym or nom de guerre of Shala. I'd like to briefly address Your Honours, and I say briefly, on the background and history of Kosovo. All peoples, all countries, are shaped by their history, by the ebb and flow of empires, by the providence that they enjoy, and by the misfortune that they must suffer. In the countries of the former Yugoslavia, history is ever present and inescapable. It animates, justifies, and fuels the action, both good and ill, of all the peoples who were once part of its complex mosaic. History, of course, is a subject which must be treated very carefully within the context of an international criminal prosecution. Quarrels over the truth or the accuracy of certain historical events are a constant danger. Nevertheless, a brief overview, I think, would be helpful for you. For generations, Serbs and Albanians have disagreed over the true history of Kosovo and the cultural ownership of the region, and both have legitimate historical claims to the area. What is true is that for the best part of a thousand years, Serbs and Albanians have lived both peacefully and in conflict in what is today Kosovo. Albanians state that they are the original inhabitants being descendents of the ancient Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond Illyrians. The Serbs state that Kosovo was at the heart of an ancient medieval kingdom. They buttress these claims by pointing to the Orthodox monasteries and churches which dot the landscape. A key date in Kosovo's history is the 28th of June, 1389. Have no fear, Your Honours, we're not going to go century by century to the present day, but it's worth mentioning this. According to classical Serbian history, on this date, the Serbian prince Lazar fought invading Ottoman Turks at Kosovo Polje, the field of black birds, and he was defeated. Although Lazar's death was celebrated as a glorious sacrifice, this defeat opened the gates to a Turkish advance which would only be stopped at the gates of Vienna some 300 years later. This single event has exercised a powerful grip on Serbian imagination, and the call to avenge Kosovo was an emotional one during the nineteenth century with the re-awakening of Serbian national identity. For many Serbs even today, Kosovo is regarded in the same way as we British see Runnymede or the Americans Valley Forge. It is a central part of their cultural and religious identity, as well as being the ancient and historical homeland of a majority Albanian population. The Ottomans ruled Kosovo for the best part of 500 years. They brought with them the Islamic faith. Albanians converted in large numbers, Serbs to a much lesser extent. Over this same period, many Serbs migrated from Kosovo. The beginning of the twentieth century saw the Serbs regain control of Kosovo from the Ottoman Turks during the Balkan wars. Terrible crimes were committed against the Albanian population. The First World War would find the Serbs defeated in Kosovo and reprisals against their retreating army and Serb civilians. At the end of those tragic four years, the Serbs would return and there were then counter-reprisals against the Albanian population. Throughout the interwar years, the Serbs tried to reverse the population in balance in Kosovo by sending Serb settlers to the area. During the Second World War, Serbs, especially the settlers, were driven out. The end of the war saw the creation of communist Yugoslavia, with Kosovo a province within the young nation. Albanians had hoped for a new Albanian state incorporating Kosovo. This was not to be. And their protests were brutally put down by the communist regime. In the 1950s and 1960s, Kosovo's autonomy within Yugoslavia was so diluted that by the early 1960s the province was under direct Serb as opposed to federal rule. Tens of thousands of Albanians were literally expelled from Kosovo. In the 1960s, Marsal Tito eased Serb control in the province and enhanced the rights of the Albanian population. In 1974, the province was granted full autonomy which gave it almost the same rights as Yugoslavia's six republics. In the post-1974 period, the Albanians were placed on a more equal footing with the Serbs and were able to occupy leading positions in both government and business in the province. From this time on, Serbs complained of harassment by Albanians, who will also demanding the status of a full republic for the province. By 1981 100.000 Serbs had left Kosovo. Serbs were increasingly worried because, thanks to Serb immigration and a high Albanian birth rate, the proportion of Serbs in the province had now fallen to a mere one for every nine Albanians. In 1981, there were large-scale riots by Kosovar Albanian students over living conditions at the University of Pristina. These riots escalated into calls for the independence of Kosovo. Following on from these riots, the repression of the Kosovar Albanian population commenced, with hundreds of arrests and ongoing security operations by the JNA and police to try and maintain order in Kosovo. After release from prison, many Kosovar Albanians emigrated to Switzerland and Germany, where the LPK, or Popular Movement of Kosovo, was formed with the aim of achieving freedom for the Albanian people in Kosovo through an armed uprising. The LPK was the forerunner of the KLA. From 1981 to 1987, tensions between the Serb and Albanian communities in Kosovo increased with claim and counter-claim. The Kosovar Serb community became more and more isolated and many felt obliged to leave for Serbia proper. The press on both sides fuelled the difficulties in Kosovo. Slobodan Milosevic then exploited the tensions in Kosovo and rose to power on the back of Serb indignation over the perceived siege-like status of Serbs in Kosovo. By 1990, Milosevic had abolished the limited autonomy that Kosovo enjoyed, installed Serbs in positions of leadership in the province and the Albanian language and culture were repressed. During this period, the LDK, or Democratic League of Kosovo, became a non-violent platform from which Albanians could challenge Serb rule in Kosovo. Hundreds of Albanians -- hundreds of thousands of Albanians joined this movement. Mr. Ibrahim Rugova, the current president of Kosovo, was in fact the LDK's first leader. By 1995, 1996, there was a growing disillusionment with the LDK policy of non-violent resistance both from within the LDK itself and from outside it. The Dayton Peace Agreement in 1995 failed to address the issue of Kosovo and the Albanian people in Kosovo felt betrayed. Support for the LPK and an armed uprising against the Serbs grew. The LPK funded attacks on Serb security forces from 1992 onwards. It organised military training in Albania. The LPK and the emergent KLA attacked police targets, killing police officers, both Serbs and Albanians. Serb refugee centres housing Serbs who had fled the conflict in other parts of Yugoslavia, were targeted. Serb unease and anger increased in the region and the reaction of the security forces intensified. Large numbers of Albanians were harassed, detained, and mistreated by Serb security forces. Albanians were taken into custody and detained without trial. Some died in police custody. In 1997, Albania itself collapsed into anarchy and military arsenals were broken into and robbed. Weapons were now available in large quantities to Kosovar Albanians who wanted to bring the fight to the Serbs. The KLA had existed since 1993, but it was the growing belief in armed resistance to Serb rule, the sudden availability of weapons from Albania, and the increasingly harsh actions of the Serb security forces which led to their rapid and effective expansion in 1997 and 1998. In February 1998, the Drenica region, a stronghold of the KLA at the time, was targeted by Serb security forces who had the aim of neutralising the KLA in the area. In the process, they killed a number of Albanian women and children. Serb security operations on the Albanian border to interdict weapons supplies to the KLA had the same results. Civilians fled and some were killed. Villages -- Albanian villages were looted and destroyed. The KLA began to establish checkpoints on roads throughout the region. Serb civilians living in these areas felt isolated and afraid. Many fled to Serbia itself or to areas of greater Serb concentration in the province. Social and business interaction between the two communities dwindled and died. And so the province rapidly spiralled into brutal ethnic conflict. It is in this context, Your Honours, against this backdrop, that the crimes in the indictment took place. It is fair to say of Kosovo that it is a place which has always remained on the periphery of those states and empires who claim sovereignty in the region, so the presence of state and state apparatus has always been very limited. Loyalties beyond family, clan, or local village community have always been traditionally unstable or weak, and you will see that in this case as the evidence unfolds. If I could now briefly address you on the issue of armed conflict. You'll see two paragraphs from the indictment, paragraphs 4 and 18, in front of you. The indictment contains charges under Article 3 and Article 5 only of the Statute, war crimes and crimes against humanity respectively. It is settled in the jurisprudence of this Tribunal that Article 3, violations of the laws and customs of war, and Article 5, crimes against humanity, can be committed in both internal and international armed Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond conflicts. The Prosecutor expressly pleads in paragraph 4 of the second amended indictment that after years of increasing tension and violence, armed conflict commenced between Serb forces and the KLA in early 1998. Taking paragraphs 4 and 18 together, we say that throughout the period of the indictment, an internal armed conflict existed between the forces of the then Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the KLA, or Kosovo Liberation Army. All three accused state in their pre-trial briefs that they do not accept that a state of internal armed conflict, as that phrase is generally understood in international criminal law, existed between the forces of the then FRY, Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and the forces of the KLA for the relevant period. The legal test to determine whether an armed conflict existed at the relevant time was first set out by the Appeals Chamber in the first case to be heard by the Tribunal, the Prosecutor and Tadic. And for the purposes of my opening, that test can be summarised as follows: The Prosecutor must show protracted armed violence between governmental authorities and organised armed groups. This calls for presentation of evidence by the Prosecutor and, respectfully, scrutiny by you, of the organisation of the parties to the conflict, firstly; and secondly, consideration of the intensity of the conflict. It is worthwhile, I think, Your Honours, for a moment to look at the guidance given by the Appellate Chamber, now nearly ten years ago, in Tadic. In the interlocutory appeals decision subsequently applied by the Trial Chamber in trial of Dusko Tadic it was stated that the temporal and geographical scope of both internal and international armed conflicts extends beyond the exact time and place of hostilities. And that you will find, Your Honours, at paragraph 67 of the appeals decision. What is the significance of this? Well, the Appeals Chamber realised that in order to sensibly assess the nature of a conflict, one cannot limit one's attention to contextual events at or around the time and place of the specific offences. In the instant case before you, I would, respectfully, submit to you that you must not only look at events in and around Lapusnik from May to July of 1998, but you must also respectfully direct your minds to the evidence of events both before and after the summer of 1998 which took place outside Lapusnik and the municipality of Glogovac in determining whether an armed conflict was taking place at the time period relevant to the indictment. And I mean specifically referring to Kosovo, not the whole of Yugoslavia, but certainly I would respectfully submit that you would direct your minds to evidence of armed conflict going on in other area areas of Kosovo apart from the municipality of Glogovac. What of the evidence? Firstly, in respect of the organisation of the parties to the conflict. In a conflict, logically there are two sides. In this conflict, on one side there was the Serb police. And as the conflict accelerated in intensity, the VJ, the Yugoslav army. On the other side was the KLA, the Kosovo Liberation Army. Dealing first with the Serb forces, you will hear evidence that many of the police engaged were specialised combat units, not exclusively regular police, which is a sign of how seriously the Serb authorities regarded the threat from the KLA. The VJ was at first deployed in the border regions. And if you look at the map in front of you, you'll see that my colleague is showing you the border regions between Albanian and Kosovo. The VJ was deployed in this region trying to stem the flow of weapons and materiel from Albania into Kosovo. As 1998 progressed, the army was increasingly used to bring the fight to the KLA inside Kosovo's borders. We do not anticipate that the level of organisation of the Serb forces will be disputed by the Defence. However, evidence of Serb police and army, organisation and operation, I would respectfully submit to you is important so the Court can assess the amount of military assets, the amount of police assets, that the KLA was engaging by the summer of 1998. The evidence is relevant not only to assess the organisation and effectiveness of the KLA, but also reflects on the intensity of the conflict itself. What of the KLA itself? The Prosecutor does not dispute that in 1998 the KLA was a developing army. One cannot equate the KLA of 1998 to a modern, well-organised NATO military force. We do not dispute that until the late summer of 1998 the KLA was based on regional areas strongly loyal to local commanders. In the instant case, Fatmir Limaj, or Celiku, being the local regional commander. But a modern, sophisticated, mature level of organisation is not necessary for the purposes of this legal jurisdictional test. If that were the requirement, if that were the jurisdictional requirement, then one can realistically speculate that many conflicts around the world would be beyond the reach of international criminal law. You will hear evidence in this case from an international witness and a retired army officer that by the summer of 1998 the KLA was sufficiently well organised to have recognisable operational areas, logistical support in the forms of arms, munitions, and uniform resupply from Albania, to operate rudimentary headquarters throughout Kosovo, to recruit and train soldiers, and by May/June of 1998, to control the passage along arterial roads within Kosovo itself, which gave them control of territory. So they were holding ground, which is what armies do. Evidence of members of the KLA will corroborate the fact that by the summer of 1998 the KLA was sufficiently well organised to mount sustained military operations in many parts of Kosovo. The Prosecution will be offering into evidence a number of KLA communiques, or public statements from the end of 1997 and throughout 1998. In these statements, the KLA emphasised on a number of occasions that it was an organised military force conducting military operations as opposed to terrorist attacks. Here you will see, Your Honours, one statement from the 11th of July of 1998. The name of the individual bracketed, Krasniqi, was the then spokesman for the KLA. I will let you obviously read all of it. I've put the whole quote in so as to give it context. But if I could read the last sentence: "Under our present circumstances, no kind of Sinn Fein can be accepted and we will not even begin to resemble the IRA," referring to the Irish Republican Army. "We are fighting for national liberation, the UCK," which is the acronym but in the Albanian language for the KLA, "is a liberation army and a regular military formation. It is not an organised or group that goes in for small-scale actions. Our operations are rather large and bear a greater resemblance to those of a regular army." So at this time, in July of 1998, the KLA itself is declaring itself to be an organised military formation. Most important, we know that by June of 1998, the first accused in this case, Mr. Fatmir Limaj, believed that the KLA was an organised structure with an authentic political and military structure, because he said so. And I'm about to play a video, and underneath it you'll see that it is subtitled. And this is an extract, and I'd ask you to follow the subtitles underneath.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So, Fatmir Limaj at this time, you've just seen, declared that the KLA was an organised structure with an authentic political and military structure. Now, we know that this statement is referring to the period of June of 1998, because you will recall when you read that, that Mr. Limaj referred to the first appearance of Mr. Krasniqi. And if I could show you this communique dated the 12th of June, 1998, you will see that this is a communique announcing that the Kosovo Liberation Army, or the KLA General Staff, had decided to appoint Professor Jakup Krasniqi as its spokesperson or spokesman. And this statement we know, because it's dated, is from 12 June 1998. So Fatmir Limaj's statement on the organisation of the KLA is linked to this time period, is linked to June of 1998, when he declared that the KLA was an organised military structure. Both Fatmir Limaj and Isak Musliu state in their pre-trial briefs, Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond at paragraph 17, that in 1998, the then Prosecutor of the International Criminal Tribunal, Louise Arbour, stated that she did not know whether the KLA constituted an organised military force answerable to the Geneva Conventions. I cannot find that statement, but I will show you what I have found. And if I could show you this next document. This is a public statement made by the Prosecutor on the 10th of March of 1998. And it's regarding the Tribunal's jurisdiction over Kosovo. I won't read it all to you, but you'll see the very last line, and she is referring to her mandate or jurisdiction, which she'd already set out: "This jurisdiction is ongoing and covers the recent violence in Kosovo." So that was the position of the Prosecutor on the 10th of March of 1998. Now, the issues I know are linked, the organisation of the conflict and the intensity of the conflict, but if I can now move on more specifically to the second part of the test, the intensity of the conflict. On the 31st of March of 1998, the Security Council, acting under its Chapter 7 powers, considered that the situation in Kosovo was so serious as to constitute a threat to international peace and security. And in front of you, you can see that document. And here the Security Council is condemning the use of excessive force by Serb police against civilians and peaceful demonstrators in Kosovo, as well as all acts of terrorism by the Kosovo Liberation Army, or any other group or individual, and all external support for terrorist activity in Kosovo. If I could have the next slide. This same resolution also decided that states should not supply weapons either to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia or, in fact, to the Kosovo Liberation Army, although the KLA is not specifically referred to there, it refers to providing military materiel and equipment for terrorist activities. Most importantly in this document is the last paragraph, which we could display now, which urged the then Prosecutor, Louise Arbour, to begin gathering information on violence in Kosovo that may fall within the jurisdiction of the ICTY. It also advises the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia to cooperate with the Tribunal. So that was the position, essentially, of the Prosecutor and the Security Council in March of 1998. Now, on the 7th of July, the Prosecutor wrote to an organisation called the Contact Group, which you may remember, which is a group of states that were essentially keeping a watch over Kosovo. This is a letter that she wrote to the then ambassador, the United States ambassador to the United Nations, and this is after several months of investigation into crimes in the region where she confirmed that the situation in Kosovo met the legal definition of an armed conflict, triggering the Tribunal's jurisdiction in the region. Now, this was clearly a retrospective declaration based on several months of investigation and work within Kosovo and was referring to crimes that had already been committed in 1998. Security Council Resolution 1199 of 23rd September 1998 noted this letter from the Prosecutor of the ICTY and also expressed the view that the situation in Kosovo represented an armed conflict within the terms of the mandate of the Tribunal. Now, these representations by the Prosecutor, while not proving that armed conflict existed, certainly, in my respectful submission, gets us part of the way there and certainly disproves the Defence assertion in their pre-trial brief that this office and the then Prosecutor believed in the summer of 1998 that there was no armed conflict in Kosovo. It's also interesting to note that by September of 1998, the Security Council was describing the fighting in Kosovo as intense and was expressing grave concern about reports of increasing violations of international humanitarian law. Security Council involvement continued and increased throughout 1998 and culminated in June of 1999 with Resolution 1244, which I've already referred to, the establishment of the United Nations interim administration in Kosovo. By the 14th of August of 1999, all Yugoslav forces had withdrawn from Kosovo and 40.000 NATO troops had deployed into the region. Evidence will be heard from an international witness and a former army officer present in Kosovo and charged with monitoring the escalation of the conflict, that over the time period of the indictment, from May to July of 1998, the conflict expanded geographically and in its seriousness and intensity. Members of the Yugoslav army and the Serb police will corroborate this witness in confirming that in the relevant part of 1998, war escalated in the region. The highly respected Human Rights Watch organisation spend much of 1998 documenting human rights abuses in Kosovo. And if we could have the next slide up. I think this speaks for itself. I'll read it, if I may, into the transcript: "The applicability of Common Article 3 and Protocol II to the conflict in Kosovo. The hostilities between the UCK and government forces had, by February 28th, 1998, reached a level of conflict to which the obligations of Common Article 3 apply. Given the subsequent intensity of the conflict from March to September, Human Rights Watch is also evaluating the conduct of the UCK and government forces based on the standards enshrined in Protocol 2 of the Geneva Conventions." We will present this report to you and this finding through a witness from Human Rights Watch. While, of course, again I emphasise, Your Honours, the Court is not bound by the finding of this international organisation, I would submit that this evidence is relevant, its probative, it's presented by a non-partisan group with vast experience and expertise of conflicts and their nature around the globe. Finally, members of the KLA and, as I've already stated to you, members of Serb forces certainly believed that by the summer of 1998 they were engaged in an armed conflict, and we will present evidence to that effect from both parties. And I'll just show to you -- it's a long document, and I don't intend reading all of it. But the interesting thing about this is that it's a KLA communique on the right-hand side of the page of the 13th of May of 1998, and on the left-hand side of the screen, you see a report from the command of the Pristina Corps, which was the main VJ formation present in Kosovo during this troubled time. And you can see that, on the left-hand side of the page, General Pavkovic, who was the commander of the Pristina Corps, who's been charged by the Tribunal with crimes during 1999, he is saying that the security situation in Kosovo is getting more and more complex every day due to the operations of Albanian terrorists, whose increasingly frequent attacks on Ministry of Interior members, citizens of Serbian nationality, and Siptar's Albanians loyal to the system are sowing fear and uncertainty. And if you go to the next box on that page, I won't read all of it, but it's worth mentioning, I think: "By their manner of operation and application of intelligence and security, engineering and logistic support measures, the terrorist forces are increasingly taking on the attributes of a military organisation and are setting up units from platoon to company." If we could go over to the next page. The document on the right remains the same. The document on the left is the second page of the report. Here you can see General Pavkovic is estimating that by May, the KLA held about 30 per cent of the territory in the country. And you'll see at the bottom of that highlighted paragraph that the Siptar, the Albanian terrorists have large quantity of weapons of various calibres and other equipment for guerrilla warfare. They have problems with ammunition shortages, which is why further attempts at forced entry over the state border from the directions of Albania and Macedonia are to be expected. If you look at the document on the right-hand side, you will see, and I won't go through all of this, we'll deal with it in more detail with a witness, but here the KLA is setting out the military operations which General Pavkovic is speaking about in this report. So Pavkovic, the VJ general, is basically responding to military operations being carried out by the KLA which are specified in this communique on the right-hand side. If we could go to the next slide. And now I've just put four Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond completeness sake the signature and stamp box of General Pavkovic, who, as I say, has been charged by the Tribunal. Mr. President, what time would you like me to go until?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We would normally think of breaking at about 20 minutes to the hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you. If I could now address you on paragraph 19 of the indictment. All acts and omissions charged as crimes against humanity were part of a widespread and systematic attack direct against the Serb civilian population and perceived Albanian collaborators. Counts 1, 3, 5, 7, and 9 charge the accused with crimes against humanity. The evidence in support of those counts is identical to that evidence which we offer for the charges under violations of the laws and customs of war. Crimes against humanity, like violations of the laws and customs of war, must be committed in the context of an armed conflict. Article 5, as Your Honours know, also requires proof that the perpetrator must know that the acts, his acts, constitute part of a pattern of widespread or systematic crimes directed against a civilian population and know that his acts fit into such a pattern. I mention this, Your Honours, because the accused dispute this allegation. They dispute that these crimes were part of a widespread and systematic attack on the population. So I will briefly address you on this requirement. The Stakic judgement, following -- Stakic trial judgement, following Kunarac, identified factors which indicate a widespread or systematic attack, noting in particular the consequences of the attack upon a targeted population, the number of victims, the number of acts, the nature of the acts, the possible participation of officials or authorities, and any identifiable pattern of crimes. Now, the Simic judgement confirmed that there is in fact no requirement in customary international law that acts which form part of the attack be connected to a policy or a plan. So that very briefly is the law, and the law is set out in more detail in our pre-trial brief. Human Rights Watch, in a report documenting breaches of international humanitarian law in 1998, to which I've already referred, stated that from February to early September 1998, the KLA had violated the laws of war by taking civilian hostages and committing summary executions. While the report contains statements by KLA officials condemning kidnapping and human rights abuses, it also cites to an announcement by the KLA spokesman, Jakup Krasniqi, in July of 1998, who readily acknowledged that civilians connected to the army or the police had been kidnapped by the KLA and that so-called Albanian collaborators had been targeted. And this is the announcement here that was made by Krasniqi. It's not entirely unequivocal, to be fair, and for that reason I'll read the sections out that I've highlighted. This is what he said in July of 1998, and you'll recall that this is the gentleman who was the spokesman for the KLA, appointed in June of 1998: "First of all, Serbian forces, whether the police, the military, or armed civilians, are our enemy. From the start, we had our own internal rules for our operations. These clearly lay down that the UCK recognises the Geneva Conventions and the conventions governing the conduct of warfare. We do not go in for kidnapping, even if some people have suffered, these have been more Albanian collaborators than Serbian civilians. We do not deal with civilians, and we return those whom we take as prisoners of war. Those we have kidnapped are either announced in a list or reported to be executed, but we do not behave in a base fashion like Serbia." So not an entirely unequivocal statement, but nevertheless an acknowledgment, in July of 1998, by the spokesperson for the KLA, that they had kidnapped individuals who were either announced in a list or reported as executed. So based on the KLA's own public relations mechanisms, we know that at a central level the KLA knew and publicly confirmed that there were kidnappings and executions taking place. The Prosecutor will offer specific evidence of an Albanian man abducted by members of the KLA and murdered just over a month after Jakup Krasniqi made this announcement. Now, this you can see on the screen in front of you, is an execution warrant. The actual warrant is the manuscript document on the right-hand side, the translation is on the left-hand side, and I have blown this up. And this is what the document stated. This was found on the body of this man that was murdered. I will go into detail about this: "For collaborating with the occupier and spreading anti-Albanian propaganda, causing fear, panic, and hatred in the name of the Albanian people, and in the name of our war of liberation, Ramiz Hoxha [phoen], from Belanica is sentenced to death as a traitor to the nation. Such a fate awaits any other traitor." Now, this death of Mr. Hoxha from Belanica was then confirmed in the press, and you can see that here. Ramiz Hoxha, from Belanica village, executed earlier by the KLA, as well as being in long-term coordination with Agim Krasniqi [phoen], a member of the KLA Presidency. The LDK Presidency. My apologies. Now, the body of this man was found with the execution warrant, the document that I showed you before this one, attached, as I say, stating that he had been executed as a traitor. No evidence exists of any trial for treason, nor is there any evidence that Mr. Hoxha was in fact a traitor. You've seen the newspaper report which subsequently confirms this man's death. Human Rights Watch estimated that by the end of 1998 well over a hundred Serbs, and probably many more, had been abducted by the KLA from Orahovac. A number of these Serbs were released, and a number simply vanished. In July of 1998, a group of Serbs were abducted and held by armed Albanians in Malisevo. One escaped, the fate of the other prisoners is unknown. And the Human Rights Watch report goes on to list the abduction of other Serbs, Roma and Albanians, throughout 1998. The expert witness, Stephanie Schwander-Sievers, will confirm that it was well known in the summer of 1998 that those members of the Albanian civilian population who are against Serb rule did not unconditionally support the KLA were brutally dealt with by the KLA. In December of 1998, Susan Ringaard Pedersen, a Dane working for the OSCE in Kosovo met with Serbs from all over Kosovo who were giving accounts of missing persons allegedly kidnapped by the KLA in the summer of 1998. OSCE, the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe, received reports of missing Kosovar Albanians and Romas. Ms. Pedersen eventually met with the KLA commander in the Lapusnik zone who confirmed to her that the KLA did in fact have Kosovar Albanians in custody who were either collaborators or criminals. Ms. Pedersen was referred to a gentleman by the name of Fahti [phoen] who was described as the head of the military police of the KLA. Fahti confirmed that the KLA had individuals in custody, and he confirmed that prisoners were kept in private houses and moved, depending on Serb military advances. Now, we know that this is absolutely consistent with what happened in the Lapusnik camp in 1998. The camp was a makeshift affair located in agricultural and domestic premises and it was moved. The prisoners were moved once Serb forces advanced into the area. Ms. Ringaard, who will give evidence to the Court, asked this Fahti for a list of prisoners at her meeting. She never received one. Members of the Serb security forces will corroborate by documents and oral testimony a well known and widespread policy in the summer of 1998 of the kidnapping of Serb and Albanian citizens by elements within the KLA. So the evidence, Your Honours, will paint a picture that as far as the specific crimes that were committed in Lapusnik are concerned, they are part of conduct which can be categorised as either widespread or systematic. Abductions were carried out over a period of months. Abductions were carried out over a fairly broad geographical area. Both Serbs and Albanians were targeted. The individuals abducted were brutally Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond treated and murdered over this three months. International observers from OSCE, from Human Rights Watch, identified a pattern of abductions of Serbs and Albanians in parts of Kosovo in the summer of 1998. High officials, a high official within the KLA in July of 1998 and later in 1999 readily acknowledged that individuals were kidnapped, imprisoned, and in certain instances executed, showing at least an awareness of events on the ground, if not a condoned policy. Serb security officials reported throughout this period a pattern of abductions and killings by the KLA of Serbs and Albanians. Mr. President, I note it's 20 to and it's a convenient point for me, if it is for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will have the first break now, resuming at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Just before you continue, Mr. Cayley, could I indicate that to this moment, the reports the Chamber has received about the matter that was raised this morning and which has been the subject of submissions by Defence counsel earlier, is not progressing satisfactorily, and for that reason, the Chamber would now formally order that the Registrar take all steps necessary to ensure that the accused in this trial are not blindfolded during their movement between the detention facility and this Tribunal. We hope that, armed with that order, better progress may prove possible. Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I've been requested if I can go more slowly. So I'm going to move a bit more slowly than I was. I hope I wasn't going too quickly beforehand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The need to translate, as I understand, progressively from one to another to another language, undoubtedly places great demands on the people trying to keep up with you. So I think that would be a good move.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I'd like to briefly address Your Honours on the nature and identity of the victims in this case. The victims in this case were Serbs and Albanians. Serbs were specifically targeted because they were Serbs, because they were identified with the ethnicity of the security forces in Kosovo. All of the Serbs except for one were civilians. One was a non-commissioned officer in the VJ, the Yugoslav army, Stamen Genov, who was in fact an ethnic Bulgarian, but a Yugoslav, serving in the Yugoslav army. And I will deal with the circumstances of his murder later in my opening. Some of the Serb victims were refugees who had been relocated to Kosovo from other parts of Yugoslavia. So they, for whatever reason, well, war was the principal reason why they had become refugees from other parts of Yugoslavia. They had been relocated by the authorities in Belgrade to Kosovo. But most of the Serb victims were in fact Kosovar Serbs, ethnic Serbs born and brought up in Kosovo itself. The Albanians who were targeted by the KLA we have referred to in our indictment as perceived collaborators. I emphasise the word "perceived" because the evidence in this case will show that Kosovar Albanians were often arrested for having had social contacts with the Serb community. They might have opposed Serb actions in Kosovo but disagreed with KLA methods. Another Albanian might have been a former state employee, a forest worker, a former policeman. None of this, none of this, of course, legitimises the brutality and killing that took place in Lapusnik between May and July of 1998. Now, if I may, Your Honours, I would like to address you on the law and, more broadly, more fully, in respect of the evidence for each count in the indictment. I've already stated that the Prosecutor relies only on Articles 3 and 5 throughout the indictment. The general legal requirements of crimes against humanity and violations of the laws and customs of war are found in paragraphs 100 to 109 of the Prosecutor's pre-trial brief. None of the accused challenge the Prosecutor's characterisation of the law. Of course they challenge the evidence. So I would, most respectfully, refer you to those paragraphs in the Prosecutor's pre-trial brief. The only areas of dispute on the law between the Prosecution and the Defence I will, and I indeed have addressed you on. Counts 1 and 2, imprisonment. Count 1 charges all three accused with a crime against humanity; specifically, imprisonment. In essence, the law says this: You cannot imprison an individual in wartime without justification. And even if you have justification, you cannot maintain confinement unless there is compliance with the procedural safeguards of the Geneva Conventions. The evidence will show in this case that there was no lawful basis for imprisonment. As for compliance with the safeguards of the Geneva Conventions, it barely justifies comment. They were never followed. Cruel treatment, count 2. In count 2, we charge the unlawful detention in this case as cruel treatment, a violation of the laws and customs of war under Article 3 of the Statute. The legal definition of cruel treatment was intentionally drafted widely to encompass all serious unlawful harm that non-combatants might be subjected to in warfare. The definition is: An act or omission which causes serious mental harm or physical suffering or injury or constitutes an attack on human dignity. And it must be committed against a person taking no active part in hostilities. Now, whilst unlawful imprisonment has not yet been categorised by Chambers within the Tribunal as forming cruel treatment, the jurisprudence clearly demonstrates that the courts have considered matters on a case-by-case basis and that the offence of cruel treatment is part of a group of core protections found in Common Article 3 of all of the Geneva Conventions. My submission to you is that to arbitrarily abduct and imprison any person taking no active part in hostilities, with no legal justification, no access to legal advice, no respect of the minimum safeguards of the Geneva Conventions, no indication to the prisoner why he is being detained, for how long he will be detained, where all around him there is death and violence is, at the very least, a serious attack on human dignity and warrants classification as cruel treatment and a violation of the laws and customs of war. Now, the three accused, while again of course taking issue with us on our evidential basis, do not take issue with us on the assertion that unlawful imprisonment is a form of cruel treatment. The evidence in this case will show that there was no legal basis for the abduction and imprisonment of any of the victims. Persons were arrested and imprisoned because they were Serbs or because they were Kosovar Albanians, who were arbitrarily regarded as collaborators. There was no evidential basis presented at the time for this classification. In no case were the safeguards of Article 43 of the Geneva Conventions met. The evidence concerning abduction and imprisonment is remarkably consistent with respect to each subset of victims with respect to the Albanian victims and with respect to the Serb victims. All of the Serbs were abducted in similar circumstances; the same can be said for the Kosovar Albanian victims. So while you will hear evidence in this trial of the abduction and imprisonment of a number of victims, in my opening, I will limit myself to providing an example to you from each ethnic group. Without wishing to repeat myself too often, some general comments: Individuals were abducted and taken to Lapusnik from May to July of 1998. At the end of July of 1998, as a result of Serb military operations in the area, the camp was evacuated and the remaining prisoners, in equal measure, were either released or executed. Only Albanian prisoners were released. By this time, all of the Serb prisoners, apart from two Serbs, had been murdered. And you will hear those two Serbs. They will be witnesses in this case. Most victims were transported to the Lapusnik camp by vehicle. Often victims were tied and blindfolded by placing sacks or blankets over their heads. In the worst instances, victims were placed in the boots or trunks of a motor vehicle and forced to remain there for hours on end whilst making their journey to the camp. Many of those abducted were severely beaten on their way to the Lapusnik camp. Some so seriously, they could no longer walk; in at least one instance, until they were beaten absolutely senseless. This is an account of one man whose fate was to be executed on the closure of the camp but who managed to survive. You will hear his story in this courtroom. He will be a witness in this case. Rizah Rexhaj is from the village of Petrov, and you can see the village of Petrov is marked on the map and you can see Lapusnik here in the red square. So Lapusnik is here, Petrov is here, highlighted with the yellow highlighter. A few days after the 4th of July of 1998, Rizah Rexhaj's 60-year-old father, Hetem, a farmer, a civilian, was taken by the KLA and unlawfully imprisoned in the Lapusnik camp. Rizah, the subject of this account, searched for his father for two weeks, trying to speak with local officials in the KLA to find some news of his father's fate. He was directed to Celiku, the first accused in this case, Fatmir Limaj, to secure his father's release, but all to no avail. Nobody would help him. Very late one night, a group of armed KLA soldiers arrived by vehicle at the family house in Petrov. He was arrested, placed in a vehicle, his head covered, and he was driven to the Lapusnik camp. The gates of the prison were opened by the third accused, Haradin Bala. Rizah was made to turn over all of his valuables to Haradin Bala, together with his belt and shoelaces. He was placed in a room in the main house in the camp. There were other prisoners there. Haradin Bala asked Rizah why he was looking for his father. And then proceeded to beat him so severely that he became unconscious. Rizah witnessed a man who was in fact murdered, called Shaban Hoti, also being beaten. His arms and legs secured by chains, covered in blood, were set about by three KLA soldiers, stamping on him, kicking him, like savages. You will hear the full description of this senseless butchery from Rizah Rexhaj when he testifies in this case. Sport for guards. Shaban Hoti was a professor and a linguist. His only offence was to have worked as an interpreter for a group of journalists of whom the KLA disapproved. Rizah Rexhaj was constantly forced to witness this kind of violence, as well as being beaten himself by both Haradin Bala and the second accused, Isak Musliu. On one occasion, Rizah Rexhaj saw Fatmir Limaj at the camp. At a later stage, Rizah Rexhaj was moved to the stable where he stayed until he left Lapusnik at the end of July, in the face of the Serb military advance. At this time, Haradin Bala, under orders from Klecka and Fatmir Limaj took the remaining 20-odd prisoners and marched them to the place I've marked on the map here, Berisa. You can see Berisa marked; you can also see Lapusnik is marked. Half of the prisoners were released and ten murdered by firing-squad, led by Haradin Bala. Rizah Rexhaj was supposed to be executed that day on the mountainside, but his survival and courage is actually why we're all here today. He had the courage to come forward, identify the accused, and show UNMIK the site of the killing. This is how the bodies were recovered and identified. And I will give you more detail of that later in my opening. His father, Hetem Rexhaj, who he had originally gone to search for, who disappeared, he saw for the last time on the 26th of July. His father had been kept in another part of the camp. When the prisoners were all marched from Lapusnik to Berisa, his father was in the group, so he saw his father at that time. His father was executed on the mountainside. A farmer, a civilian. But his son, Rizah, would survive, and you will hear directly from him about this tragedy. Serb victims were principally abducted and imprisoned in May and June of 1998. When the camp was evacuated in July, there were only two known Serb survivors. It is their story that I will tell, but it does serve as a basis for the imprisonment of many of the Serb victims in this case. On the 29th of June of 1998, two Serbs, father and son, Vojko and Ivan Bakrac, were taken from a bus travelling from Kosovo to Belgrade in a village called Crnoljevo. You can see marked on this map in front of you. This road, essentially it comes from the south up from Suva Reka, travels through Crnoljevo, and this is the road that they would have taken on their way to Belgrade and Serbia proper. At this time, in June of 1998, Crnoljevo was the KLA stronghold, and the local commander there was subordinated to the first accused in this case, Fatmir Limaj. Many families of all ethnicities have suffered in this war in Yugoslavia, but the tragic odyssey of the Bakracs, I think, is demonstrative of the entire breakdown of this nation. Vojko, an ethnic Serb, born in Slovenia, his son Ivan, also an ethnic Serb, born in Zagreb, in Croatia, in 1979. In 1992, Serbia and Croatia were at war with each other. At the age of 13, Ivan and his family were forced to leave Zagreb and flee to Belgrade. The Serbian authorities in Belgrade found his father Vojko work in Kosovo, in Djakovica, in a hotel. The Bakracs soon realised that Kosovo was about to explode into ethnic conflict, and the family planned constantly to try and leave Kosovo and find a better life away from Yugoslavia. In June of 1998, the Bakracs will tell you that Kosovo was in crisis, that the KLA was controlling many of the roads in the province, and that it was very unsafe to travel on the roads if you were a Serb. At the time of their kidnapping by the KLA, the Bakracs were having to make a final journey to Belgrade to obtain papers and permission to leave the country for good. The bus was stopped by members of the KLA at the village of Crnoljevo, marked on the map. Father and son will say that they were removed from the bus with two other victims in this case, murdered victims, Stamen Genov, and Djordje Cuk, the man that you will recall I mentioned was a non-commissioned officer in the Yugoslav army. The second, Djordje Cuk, was a Serb civilian. Father and son were very frightened indeed, but they thought -- as they thought they were about to be killed. Mrs. Bakrac, Vojko's wife, remained on the bus. She was hysterical. Each of us can imagine the scene. On covering that Stamen Genov was in the VJ, in the Yugoslav army, the Bakracs will state to the Court that he was so badly beaten by members of the KLA that he could no longer stand on his own two feet. Ivan and Vojko Bakrac were taken along with Stamen Genov and Djordje Cuk to a location which they cannot name but which both father and son have identified from photographs as the place -- as the location which the Prosecutor says is the makeshift detention camp at Lapusnik. Ivan, the son, will identify the accused Haradin Bala as being a guard in the camp. He identified Mr. Bala from a photo spreadsheet that was presented to him during interview and confirmed to the investigator that Haradin Bala was the man that he knew as Shala in the prison camp at Lapusnik. The father, while unable to identify Haradin Bala from photographs, provides a compelling description of the third accused in this case and confirms that the man that he describes he knew as Shala, the nom de guerre of Haradin Bala. Recall, Your Honours, that Haradin Bala expressly acknowledges being called Shala but denies being in Lapusnik after late May of 1998. And there is no doubt at all, Your Honours, that the Bakracs were taken and unlawfully imprisoned in the Lapusnik camp at the end of June of 1998. Both witnesses describe very accurately the basement area of the camp, where father and son were kept with a number of other Serb and Albanian prisoners. Being Serbs from Croatia, Ivan wisely lied and said they were Croats rather than Serbs, hoping that this might save them. They believe that initially this may have saved their lives, although the KLA subsequently realised that they were Serbs from Croatia. Both witnesses will go on to explain how, after seven days, the KLA decided to release them. Father and son were forced to make a statement on a video-recording by the KLA to say how well they had been treated at Lapusnik. Then they were blindfolded, led to a vehicle, and driven to Malisevo, where they were released into the custody of the international committee for the Red Cross. I would draw your attention, Your Honours, to an interview that I've already shown to you, with Jakup Krasniqi, the official spokesman for the KLA, who on the 10th of July, 1998, stated to a newspaper in Kosovo, "Koha Ditore," the following, and I'll read to you what he said: "A few days ago, we handed over two Serbs originating from Croatia to the International Red Cross." And then he goes on to state part of the quote that I read earlier: "Those we have kidnapped are either announced in a list or reported to be executed, but we do not behave in a base fashion like Serbia." So here Jakup Krasniqi is discussing, expressly announcing the release of these two Serbs, of the Bakracs. These two men are the only known Serb survivors from the camp. Stamen Genov and Djordje Cuk were taken with them. They've never been seen again. The circumstances of their murder I will deal with later in my opening. Counts 3 to 6, torture, inhumane acts and cruel treatment. These counts, Your Honours, cover the mistreatment of prisoners at the camp, the physical abuse that was meted out to many of the victims, and also the appalling conditions in which prisoners were forced to live. The lack of proper food, the grotesque hygiene conditions and the primitive and barbaric manner in which many of the prisoners were chained up like animals and made to lie in their own excrement, unable to move or walk about. Again, while the three accused dispute the evidence, they do not dispute our characterisation of the law, and you will find that in paragraphs 112 to 121 of the Prosecutor's pre-trial brief. Counts 3 and 4 both charge torture, first as a crime against humanity. Counts 3 and 4 both charge torture, first as a crime against humanity, and secondly, as a war crime. Tribunal jurisprudence confirms that the basic elements of the offence are the same, whether torture is charged under Article 3 or under Article 5. The only distinction -- the only legal distinction between the two offences being the general legal requirements of a crime against humanity. Torture is distinguished from other forms of maltreatment on the basis of the seriousness and purpose of the attack. The purpose can be to obtain information or a confession or, indeed, to just intimidate somebody. It is worth noting, Your Honours, that the purpose need only be part of the motivation. It need not be the sole or even the predominant purpose of the attack. The Krnojelac judgement provides some useful guidance at paragraph 182, which respectfully, I think, will assist the Court in making a finding on this count. As to counts 5 and 6, we charge inhumane acts as a crime against humanity and cruel treatment as a violation of the laws and customs of war. Again, the basic ingredients of the offences are the same. The only distinction being the additional general legal requirements of a crime against humanity. What of the evidence? The evidence, Your Honours, in this case will show that while not all prisoners were beaten, those that were, were often beaten ferociously, repeatedly, and often until they fell into an unconscious state. Physical violence and the intimidation and fear which arises from it was the very essence of the regime at Lapusnik. In some instances, you will hear that prisoners were literally beaten to death. Survivors will say how they lost teeth, how they were beaten until ribs were broken, how men were literally broken down by repeated constant brutality. Prisoners were beaten with fists, stamped on, kicked, attacked with instruments. Constant fear consumed all of the prisoners. Each could see the results of the latest attack. Who would be next? How long would they be beaten for? Who would beat them? Would they survive another beating? Forensic evidence and the oral testimony of a survivor will show that in one instance a prisoner was beaten so severely that the tibia bone of his leg was literally cleaved in two. I've already stated to you that at the final execution site in Berisa, nine sets of mortal remains were uncovered by UNMIK. Those remains were examined by a forensic pathologist, a forensic anthropologist, and Professor George Maat, professor of anatomy and forensic anthropology at the University of Leiden. That forensic evidence will show together that these prisoners, these dead that were recovered at Berisa had suffered traumatic injuries to chest, forearm, lower legs, teeth, some of the injuries were described as life-threatening. All were consistent with having been stamped on, received blows from fists or other blunt-force trauma. The evidence will show, Your Honours, that those prisoners who were beaten were sometimes interrogated at the same time they were beaten. A number of prisoners will state that while they were beaten, they were interrogated by their torturers about their interaction with the Serb population in Kosovo. At other times, the evidence will demonstrate that the beatings took place as a severe form of intimidation. I will leave it respectfully to Your Honours to decide when physical violence reaches such a threshold that it becomes torture, but I would respectfully suggest some markers for you.
