Firstly, the extraordinary intensity of the beatings in this case. Secondly, the repeated nature of physical beatings or attacks on individuals. Thirdly, the state of victims after attacks. And lastly, the extended period over which attacks took place. Prisoners were often tied up when they were beaten. Sometimes they were blindfolded. Often, but not always, their torturers, KLA soldiers in Lapusnik, had their faces covered when they were engaged in this violence. But often, prisoners came to know their torturers because of the masked individual's the stature, his nickname, his nom de guerre, his voice, the way in which he went about his beatings. The other physical and mental abuse suffered by the prisoners were the conditions of the detention itself. Those prisoners in the stable, and I think tomorrow when the first witness testifies you will see these locations within the camp, you'll see what I mean by the stable. Those prisoners in the stable were essentially chained up like animals, unable to move properly, dirty, bleeding, hungry. On the provision of food and water, you will hear mixed accounts. Prisoners taken early on, it seems, suffered more than those who came later. Further, certain prisoners seem to have been targeted specially for abuse, which led to paltry rations or lack of drinking-water. Some prisoners talk about very little food or water being provided. Others say it was not good, but it was adequate. Hygiene was poor, and in my submission, deliberately so. Where prisoners were allowed to relieve themselves, as opposed to being forced to foul themselves, they had to share an overflowing and irregularly emptied bucket. There was virtually nothing in the way of medical care for the prisoners. And in a way, in a place where so much violence was inflicted on an institutional basis, it is not surprising at all that prisoners were not cared for. For many of them, for many of them, Your Honours, they were simply confined to this place with the sole intention of making them suffer as much as humanly possible. Haradin Bala is linked by a number of victims to the violence in this camp. He, it seems, was never masked. Victims knew him by name and nickname and described his appearance. Some victims recognised him from before the war. Haradin Bala was involved in directly inflicting violence himself and often stood guard while other KLA guards or soldiers did the beatings. Isak Musliu. He was the immediate commander of those engaged in the beatings and torture. He seems to have often worn a mask. Nevertheless, a number of victims name him either by his real name or nickname, as a particularly violent individual, who was often involved in the beating of prisoners. Some prisoners will describe how they were subjected to martial arts techniques, ferocious kicks and punches. These accounts are linked to a degree by completely independent evidence to Isak Musliu. In front of you, you will see a document that was recovered from Isak Musliu's house. It is a membership card of the Kosovo karate federation. And on the next slide, you will see Mr. Musliu's name. The next document is an extract from Mr. Musliu's police application form to the Kosovo police service, where he describes himself as a first-level master in karate. Fatmir Limaj was often at the camp and was seen on a number of occasions in amongst the prisoners. The ongoing violence and the conditions would have been obvious to him. Limaj knew what was going on. Indeed, he was part of it as the overall superior and approved of it. What is more, with Isak Musliu in charge at Lapusnik, Fatmir Limaj was directly responsible for what took place there. Of course, as I have said, individuals other than Haradin Bala and Isak Musliu beat and abused the prisoners. You will hear that. But that violence was simply part of a system of ill-treatment of which all three accused were a part. The acts of the other guards in the camp who are not here before you, by virtue of the joint criminal enterprise, are the acts of Fatmir Limaj, the acts of Isak Musliu, and the acts of Haradin Bala. Again, Your Honours, I emphasise to the Court, and I show you a portion of the pre-trial brief of Mr. Fatmir Limaj. Fatmir Limaj, you will see about halfway down this extract, was based in Klecka. From time to time, he would go to Lapusnik to assist with various operations. He went to Lapusnik approximately 20 times during this time. Now, that, Your Honours, is an admission by Fatmir Limaj in his pre-trial brief. Now, his position is that he came to help with ongoing military operations, and you can see that from the document. Whilst he does not acknowledge being in the camp and while there are witnesses who place him in the camp, it is also absolutely inconceivable that he went to Lapusnik to help with military operations without being aware of the camp holding all of these prisoners. The front lines at Lapusnik, the area of KLA military operations, is 350 metres away from this camp. If I could now, please, turn to the last counts in the indictment, murder, counts 7 to 10. Murder is charged in counts 7 and 9, as a crime against humanity, and in counts 8 and 10 as a violation of the laws and customs of war. As with torture, the elements of murder are the same whether charged as a crime against humanity or a violation of the laws and customs of war. The only difference being, I've said it before, I know I'm repeating myself, the additional general requirements of the crime against humanity. And you will find at paragraphs 122 to 124 the law in respect of murder. The first murder which you will find referred to in the indictment, in paragraph 29, is the killing of Ajet Gashi, and you can see his photograph before you. Limaj and Musliu are charged under Article 7(1) and 7(3) of the Statute with the unlawful killing of this individual. Ajet Gashi was a former police officer, an Albanian, who was dismissed from the police and tried on political grounds by the Milosevic regime. Ajet's brother, Shesat Gashi [phoen], says that in May of 1998 Ajet went to the KLA headquarters in Klecka. His family thought he was there working for the KLA. On hearing nothing from him, Ajet Gashi's mother made inquiry at the KLA headquarters in Likovc. She was told not to worry. But she was, so she repeated her inquiries. On her third inquiry, she was instructed by at KLA soldier at Likovc not to make any more inquiries about her son. While Ajet's brother believes that Ajet was kept in Lapusnik camp, you will also hear direct evidence from one witness who saw him in Lapusnik camp from mid-May of 1998. Ajet Gashi, like a number of other prisoners, was made to write a confessional account about his life. In some instances, we have those statements that were made by those prisoners at Lapusnik. Evidence will show that Gashi was kept in what I have described to you as the stable, an area of the compound where animals would normally be kept. He was very badly beaten, indeed. You will hear evidence of the circumstances of Gashi's execution. The evidence will show that at around the 10th of June of 1998, Ajet Gashi was taken from Lapusnik by a number of soldiers and guards from Lapusnik camp. On the Magura road at the Laletic turn-off - and I've marked that on the map for you here, Your Honors. You can see the villages of Laletic and Magura marked. On the Magura road at the Laletic turn-off, he was executed by automatic gunfire by two KLA soldiers under the command of Isak Musliu and Fatmir Limaj. The evidence will show that Ajet Gashi was murdered on military order. Evidence will be led that such an order would have gone to Lapusnik and would have come from Klecka, Fatmir Limaj's headquarters. The corpse of Ajet Gashi was found and recovered by his family near the spot where he was murdered between Magura and Laletic. Court documents and newspaper articles of the time will be produced confirming his murder. Here is one from "Koha Ditore" confirming a person killed at the Goles Pass two days ago was identified today. Reports state that this person is Ajet Kamba [phoen] Gashi from Glogovac in Malisevo. Ajet was shot with five bullets in the chest. His body remained on the roadside at the entrance to Magura for two days and had begun to decay, left there as an example to others. All of Kosovo was on notice in June of 1998 of Ajet Gashi's killing. The family recovered the body and buried it in the village cemetery in Glogovac. In 2003, the OTP, the Office of the Prosecutor, sought permission to exhume the body from its grave site in order to perform an autopsy and anthropological examination. That was duly done and the findings of that examination confirm that the cause of death was as a result of multiple gunshot wounds to trunk and head. Now, if I could turn Your Honours' attention to murder of those individuals set out in Annex 1 of the indictment. All of these men were taken by the KLA between 24 June 1998 and 26 July 1998. They were all imprisoned at Lapusnik and then murdered. All except one were civilians. All except one a Serb. As I have said, Stamen Genov, an ethnic Bulgarian and Yugoslav, was serving as a sergeant medic in the VJ but off duty when arrested. Fatmir Limaj and Isak Musliu are charged under both Article 7(1) and 7(3) of the Statute with the murder of these eight men. Here in this photograph, on the left-hand side, you see Milovan Krstic, and on the right-hand side, Miodrag Krstic. In this photograph, you see Boban Mitrovic. When they were murdered in 1998, Milovan Krstic, the first gentleman that you saw on the left-hand side, was 28 and married with two children; Miodrag Krstic was 34 and married with four children. This gentleman on the screen now, Slobodan Mitrovic, was married with twins. Milovan and Miodrag Krstic were brothers. Slobodan Mitrovic was their cousin. The three men were good friends as well as relatives. They all lived in Racak, in Suva Reka, in Kosovo. And you can see that there marked on the map. They didn't actually live in Suva Reka. They lived in a village near Suva Reka but it's in that area of Kosovo. Prior to the war, all three had married, settled down, found jobs, gone about their lives peacefully with their Albanian neighbours. Indeed, Slobodan Mitrovic had many Albanian friends and spoke the language. Slobodan, or Boban, as he was known had married Ljiljana in 1982, and 1991 the twins, Alexander and Ana, were born. In mid-June of 1998, Slobodan Mitrovic was warned by an Albanian friend that he should move his family, his young children, to Serbia because he was in grave danger. So on the 14th of June of 1998, he moved his wife, Ljiljana, and the children to relatives at Arandjelovac in Serbia. He returned to Racak in Kosovo. In June of 1998, Miodrag Krstic, who was the gentleman that you saw on the left hand photograph, the second photograph that I showed you, had been receiving urgent medical treatment in Belgrade, Serbia. On June 23rd, Milovan Krstic and Slobodan Mitrovic went to Belgrade to collect him and bring him back to his family in Kosovo. The two men had travelled via Arandjelovac in Serbia. Whilst Slobodan Mitrovic had kept in regular contact with his wife whilst they had been apart, he decided that he wanted to surprise her and the children. The security situation in Kosovo was now dreadful. Ljiljana, his wife, knew it and she pleaded with him to stay with the family in Serbia. Milovan Krstic did not want to travel back to Kosovo with his sick brother alone, so against his wife's pleas, Boban went on with him to the hospital in Belgrade. Ljiljana and the twins would never see Boban again. Milovan Krstic and Slobodan Mitrovic stayed the night of the 23rd of June of 1998 in Belgrade with relatives. Miroslav Krstic, the uncle of Milovan and Miodrag, had called them that night from Kosovo and warned them of the danger of travelling back to Suva Reka through Crnoljevo. You will recall the location where I've already indicated the Bakracs and Djordje Cuk and Stamen Genov were kidnapped by the KLA. For here there was a KLA checkpoint. Nevertheless, the next morning, the two men collected Miodrag Krstic from hospital and then the three friends started their journey back to Kosovo. Not heeding the advice of their uncle, they travelled back through Crnoljevo. The police confirmed that the three men crossed the border into Kosovo from Serbia sometime between 3.20 and 3.30 on the afternoon of the 24th of June, 1998. Sometime after this they were kidnapped in Crnoljevo by the KLA and taken to Lapusnik. And I've marked again for you on this map the location of Lapusnik, here, and the location of Crnoljevo, the KLA checkpoint, here, and the area where the village of Racak where the three men lived, is near to Suva Reka. Here all three men were seen by survivors in the cell which was the storage room in the camp at Lapusnik. These three men have never been seen since, either in Lapusnik or having been taken from Lapusnik by guards in the camp. They were murdered. Your Honours, in providing you with faded glimpses of a man's life, I'm not appealing to your emotions. I'm simply emphasising the repercussions and the damage beyond death that these three accused have caused by their acts. Ljiljana, Boban's Mitrovic's wife we'll bring to the Court so she can describe her husband for you. She describes an absolutely wonderful man who loved her and the children. He would always call them if he was away from the family. She will describe the daily battle between hope and despair that she goes through every day. She is certain that if her husband were alive over six years later, he would find a way to get to her and the children. Of course, this man is dead. But because there is no body, because his remains were almost certainly buried in secret, there is no end to this matter for this family, no end for the grief for her and the children. These people lead lives of suspended animation, where they can neither go forward for backwards, and these proceedings may at least bring closure for one family to make peace with the past and move on with the future. The next victim is a man called Miroslav Suljnic. You see his photograph here. He lived in Vidanja in Kosovo with his parents, brother, and sister. He worked in a sawmill in Doberdol village. From the 10th of May of 1998 to the 21st of May of 1998, he had worked solidly at the sawmill and had not been home. On the 21st of May, he began the journey home, sometime between 4.00 and 4.30. Miroslav arrived at the Serb MUP checkpoint at Komorane on the Pristina-Pec road. He was warned not to continue with his journey by the Serb police because he was told that the KLA had a checkpoint at Lapusnik, the location of the camp, which I've already shown to you on the map. Miroslav Suljnic had never had problems previously with his Albanian neighbours, and he believed that he was going to be safe and so he ignored the warning and carried on with his journey. At the checkpoint, at Lapusnik, he was taken by the KLA to the camp at Lapusnik where he was imprisoned. A survivor from the camp confirms his presence at Lapusnik at the end of June/beginning of July of 1998. The Serb security forces, when they retook this area at the end of July of 1998, found the following document. On the right-hand side, you can see a handwritten document, and in English, you can see the translation. So the Serb security forces found this document: "I am Miroslav Suljnic, born on 8 June 1996." It's written as that. "Worker by profession, captured by the Kosovo Liberation Army in Lapusnik on the 21st of May." As I've said, Your Honours, a number of witnesses will say that they were obliged to write a confessional account about their lives for the purposes of interrogation by members of the KLA. Jeremija Suljnic, the victim's brother, will say that this is definitely his brother's handwriting. Now, while the document states that he was born in 1996, of course, we know that Miroslav Suljnic in 1998 was a grown man; in fact, he was born in 1969. He reversed the numbers. And in a sense, such an error, in my submission, adds to the authenticity of this document. We can all of us imagine somebody very frightened indeed writing this out while imprisoned in Lapusnik camp. The family has never seen Miroslav again, for he was murdered either at Lapusnik or having been taken from Lapusnik between 24 June 1998 and 26 July 1998. The next victim is a man who you see in front of you now by the name of Zivorad Krstic. He is no relation to Milovan and Miodrag, the two that I've already referred to. This man was a retired widower living in Pristina in 1998. He was 68 years old. He had three daughters. His wife had died when the children were young, and according to his son-in-law, he had committed his life to raising his three girls. He is described by witnesses as a gentle soul who was universally liked and respected by both his Albanian and Serb neighbours. At the time of his kidnapping, he was being treated for diabetes. He had recently had eye surgery to remove cataracts from both eyes. He was a sick man. On the 23rd of June of 1998, he travelled from Pristina to a village outside Prizren to attend his brother's funeral. His brother had recently passed away. On the 25th of June, he was put on a bus by his dead brother's son, Vekmir [phoen] Krstic, to return him to Pristina. The bus left at 10.00 or 11.00 in the morning. Evening came, Your Honours, and Zivorad had not arrived in Pristina. Checks were made with the police in Prizren and the police confirmed that the bus had been stopped by the KLA in, again, the village of Crnoljevo. And you can see here, Crnoljevo, Crnoljevo. Zivorad Krstic was taken from the bus by the KLA. His identity card and the few belongings that he had with him were returned to the family. Days later, Stojan Stojanovic, Zivorad's son-in-law, heard the news that Ivan and Vojko Bakrac, the two Serbs that I referred to who were released, had also been kidnapped in Crnoljevo and that they had just been released by the KLA through the Red Cross. Stojan Stojanovic, the victim's son-in-law, made contact with the Bakracs and he showed them a photograph of his father-in-law, and they confirmed -- the Bakracs confirmed that Zivorad Krstic had indeed been in the Lapusnik camp, that he had introduced himself to them and told them who he was and where he was from. Zivorad Krstic has never been seen by his family, and it is the Prosecutor's case that he was either murdered in Lapusnik or murdered having been taken from Lapusnik by guards from the camp, a sick man returning from his brother's funeral, murdered for being a Serb. The next two victims that you can see in front of you are Stamen Genov and Djordje Cuk. Stamen Genov you see to the right in a military uniform. I've already stated to you that he was a medic in the VJ at the time of these events. The other gentleman on the left-hand side is Djordje Cuk. Djordje Cuk was a young Serb born in Croatia. In 1995, his family left Croatia because of the war in that region, and, as I've already stated to you, along with many other Serb refugees, was relocated with his parents and brother to Djakovica, in Kosovo. On the 29th of June of 1998, he was travelling by bus from Djakovica to Belgrade in the same bus carrying the Bakracs. The bus was stopped by KLA troops, as I've already said, at Crnoljevo. Everybody's papers were checked and Djordje, along with the three other men, was taken off the bus. In addition, Djordje Cuk, the ethnic Bulgarian, a serving member of the VJ, was removed with him. Stamen Genov, as it happens, was off duty and en route to see his girlfriend in Krusevac. The Bakracs will say that both Djordje and Stamen were extremely frightened. All four of the victims were taken by the KLA to a school where they were all interrogated about their background. Stamen Genov was quickly identified from his military identification papers. He and Djordje Cuk were then severely beaten. Stamen Genov was beaten until he was unconscious. Djordje Cuk was also so badly beaten that when the KLA soldiers came to move the four of them to Lapusnik, he could not stand on his own two feet. At Lapusnik, both Genov and Cuk were both beaten. Stamen Genov was subjected to particularly brutal treatment because he was a member of the Yugoslav forces. Witnesses will say that Genov was so severely beaten that eventually he begged his fellow prisoners to kill him. At the end of July of 1998, when Serb forces overran Lapusnik, copies of Genov's interrogation notes were recovered from the site, and you can see those in front of you now. I'm not going to go through them in detail. I don't know how well those appear on your screens, but the notes begin: "My name is Stamen Genov." It says where he was born, when he was born and then it proceeds to list details of the Yugoslav military garrison in Djakovica. It was at this same time - and if we could move to the next document - that the Serb security forces in Kosovo confirmed his death. And the Prosecution will produce minutes of a meeting held on the 30th of July. You can see here meetings of the joint command for Kosovo. These were meetings held by officials in the Serb army, the Serb police, and the Serb civilian administration that was set up as a joint command to deal with the crisis situation in Kosovo at the time. If we could move to the next slide. Here you see on the 30th of July the group discussing the fact that Corporal Genov was killed, referring to Stamen Genov. There's no doubt, Your Honours, from all of the accounts that you will hear that this young man, a medic in the VJ, was subjected to a level of brutality which frankly describes [sic] description. He died at or outside Lapusnik, almost certainly bludgeoned to death. Neither Djordje Cuk nor Stamen Genov have of course ever been seen again by their relatives. Both men are dead, murdered by guards from the camp at Lapusnik, either in Lapusnik or taken from Lapusnik. Sinisa Blagojevic. You see a photograph before you here now. He is the man on the right-hand side of the picture. Sinisa Blagojevic was 32 years old in June of 1998. He came from and lived in the village of Krajiste, which is a mixed Albanian Serb village in Kosovo. He was one of six children, he being the eldest and the head of the family. He was married with two small children of his own. He worked for the state as a forest guard or ranger at Lipovica and had an apartment in Vusevac [phoen] which was provided by his employer for the purposes of his work. On the 22nd of June, Sinisa was told that his apartment in Vusevac had been looted and vandalised earlier in the week. Sinisa and his family were told by the police that it was not safe to go there to inspect it, but nevertheless they went and recovered what they could from Sinisa's apartment. Sinisa kept livestock near his work apartment, and they talked about taking the livestock away with them that day. They decided not to. Instead, Sinisa would come back the next day. He set off on his tractor the next day and was never seen again by his family. The police told his brother the KLA had been active that day in Vusevac and further information indicated that a KLA checkpoint had been in the village at the time. Sinisa was in fact taken by the KLA to Lapusnik and then murdered. Again, he's never been seen again since his kidnapping. If I could now move, please, Your Honours, to Annex 2 of the indictment. These four men were murdered in mid-July 1998 at or near the Lapusnik prison camp. Just to remind you, I'm repeating what I've already said in respect of these murders, Fatmir Limaj and Isak Musliu are charged under Article 7(1) and 7(3) of the Statute. Isak Musliu and Haradin Bala and also charged with direct participation in or aiding and abetting the murder of these four individuals. The two individuals on the screen in front of you, the one on the left-hand side is a man called Jefta Petkovic and the younger man on the right-hand side is Zvonko Marinkovic. Zvonko Marinkovic was a young Serb man who lived in a village called Musutiste with his wife, Svetlana Marinkovic, and their two young children aged 8 and 3 at the time of these events. He shared the house with his brother and his brother's wife and children. You will hear from his wife that the family was a close one that enjoyed eight good years of marriage prior to his disappearance and death. He worked for a company called the Balkan company. Jefta Petkovic, the gentleman on the left, the left photograph, from the village of Racak in Suva Reka worked with Zvonko Marinkovic as a trucker driver for the Balkan company. On the 23rd of June of 1998, Zvonko telephoned his wife Svetlana to tell her he was coming home from Belgrade in a company truck with Jefta Petkovic that day. That is the last time his wife heard from him. On the 24th of June, both men were taken from the Balkan company truck near the village of Crnoljevo. Again, the same location where there was located a KLA checkpoint and taken to the KLA detention facility at Lapusnik. They were both civilians, both Serbs. Survivors from the camp identify both Zvonko and Jefta from their photographs as being present in the camp, although it is often the case that names were never known or were confused because prisoners were not always able to speak with each other. Jefta and Zvonko suffered the brutal regime that I've already described for you. Prior to the evacuation of the camp at the end of July of 1998, Zvonko Marinkovic and Jefta Petkovic were murdered. The next two victims that you see in front of you of are Agim Ademi, on the left, and Vesel Ahmeti on the right. In June of 1998, Agim Ademi and Vesel Ahmeti were both kidnapped from the village of Gorance and taken to the KLA detention facility at Lapusnik. Both men were chained up in the cowshed and both were subjected to ferocious beatings. In the middle of July, both of these men were murdered. The next individual that you see in front of you is a man by the name of Fehmi Xhema, also know as Fehmi Tafa. On the 13th of June 1998 a man named Vebi Tafa [phoen] from the village of Crnoljevo -- and just so there's no confusion, Your Honours, this is a man who is distinct from the victim. This man's name is Vebi Tafa, the victim's name is Fehmi. So a man named Vebi Tafa from the village of Crnoljevo had gone missing from his home. So again, the same location, Crnoljevo where the KLA checkpoint existed, where many of the Serbs victims were taken from vehicles. The next day, the 14th of June of 1998, his brother, Fehmi Tafa, the man in this photograph, went to look for him. Fehmi Tafa was soon detained by two KLA soldiers from the village of Crnoljevo. He was taken to the local KLA headquarters where he was tied and blindfolded and placed in a car. First of all, he was taken to the village of Klecka, where Fatmir Limaj's headquarters was located, and then he was driven to the camp at Lapusnik. He was brought out of the car and brought into a cell at Lapusnik. Sometime after the 14th of July -- 14th of June, I'm sorry, of 1998, Haradin Bala and Isak Musliu and two other soldiers came into the cell where Fehmi Tafa was being held. They told him to stand. He was tied and blindfolded. The other prisoners in the room were ordered to look away. The four guards, including Isak Musliu and Haradin Bala, took Fehmi Tafa away. Later, Haradin Bala and Isak Musliu dragged Fehmi back into the cell. He was half unconscious. He had been savagely beaten. He could barely speak. He was in a terrible state from the beating. He begged for water and complained of pains in his chest. One of the prisoners asked Haradin Bala for some water for Fehmi. It was refused. 20 minutes later, Fehmi died in his filthy cell, beaten to death. Bala, Haradin Bala, was informed that Fehmi was dead. The cell was guarded closely for 24 hours by Bala and another guard and then the body was removed by Haradin Bala and other soldiers. And finally, Your Honours, if you would turn to Annex 3. I'm sorry. If you have the indictment in front of you. But I will turn to Annex 3, where you will find the names of ten dead. The relevant paragraphs of the indictment are 34 to 37.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Finally, Your Honours -- sorry, Mr. President. May I continue? Finally, Your Honours, if I could refer you to Annex 3 of the indictment, where you will find the names of ten dead. The relevant paragraphs in the indictment are paragraphs 34 to 37. And in respect of these crimes, Fatmir Limaj and Haradin Bala only are charged under 7(1) and 7(3) of the indictment. Fatmir Limaj and Haradin Bala are charged under 7(1) of the Statute for planning, instigating, ordering, committing, or otherwise aiding and abetting; and Fatmir Limaj only is also charged under 7(3) of the Statute. On the 26th of July of 1998, an offensive was launched by Serb security forces in the area against the KLA stronghold at Lapusnik. We know this from the prisoners in the camp who heard shooting and shelling, and we also know it from Serb military documents which, if I had more time, I would show you. But we will produce them in evidence. But essentially, military reports from the Serbs demonstrating that there was an offensive in the area of Lapusnik on the 26th of July. So essentially confirming what the prisoners actually heard within the camp. As the Serb advance crept forward towards Lapusnik and the prison camp, Haradin Bala and another guard moved all of the remaining prisoners in the camp into the central compound, and you'll see that in more detail with Mr. Lehtinen's evidence when he will take you, as it were, on a visual tour within the camp. We have what's called rather unfortunately a virtual reality presentation of the camp which enables you to essentially walk through the camp as if you were there. But you will see this particular area that I'm referring to, the central compound. There were 20 individuals gathered, all of them Kosovar Albanians, as I've said, all of the Serbs, the remaining Serbs, were by this stage dead, murdered. Bala told the prisoners that they had to leave Lapusnik and that they would go towards Berisa. And you can see on the map in front of you, I've shown you where Berisa was before. I've marked it there again. And the mountains. Anybody trying to escape would be executed on the spot. The prisoners were, as you can imagine, in absolutely appalling sight. Beaten, weak, covered in their own excrement. I've already mentioned to you that one prisoner, Shyqyri Zymeri, had been beaten so savagely that his tibia was broken in two. He could not walk, and so you will hear evidence that the other prisoners had to take turns in carrying him up the hillside. This is rough terrain, Your Honours. It would have been a challenge for a fit group of individuals. These people were in no fit state to be walking up into the mountains above Lapusnik. The prisoners walked for some time, and eventually came to a spot where a forest trail crossed their path. Here you will hear evidence that Fatmir Limaj arrived with an escort and spoke with Haradin Bala for a number of minutes. Fatmir Limaj then departed, leaving behind him a KLA soldier from his own escort who would become the third member of the escort for those prisoners who were executed. The ragged group walked on and stopped near a brook and some fruit trees. Bala then divided the prisoners into two groups. The prisoners knew something was afoot. The first group, which included over ten prisoners, was taken to one side. Haradin Bala gave each of these prisoners a written authority in the name of Commander Celiku, Fatmir Limaj, stating that they had been released. This group then made their way to a KLA headquarters in Kishna Reka which you will see marked on the map there below Lapusnik. Here they were detained for a short period of time and were then transferred to a location called Kroimire, which you can also see marked on the map here, beneath Klecka. Bala returned to the remaining prisoners, those that had not been released, and called out the names of one after the other. The group was marched into a clearing in the forest by Haradin Bala and two other guards. You will recall the first guard who had been with Bala in the compound at the Lapusnik, the third guard from Fatmir Limaj's military escort. Bala was armed with an AK-47 assault rifle, as was the third soldier from Limaj's group. The other guard from Lapusnik was armed with a single-shot M-48 rifle. The group was ordered to sit in a straight line. By now, these men knew that death was very close. Bala announced that they would all be punished by death, and three soldiers then opened fire, the three soldiers then opened fire in a continuous volley. Two prisoners, sensing what was to come, reacted very quickly and ran into the very thick forest that surrounded the group. All other ten men fell to the ground in the hail of gunfire or perished. You will hear, as I've already told you, evidence from one of these survivors, Rizah Rexhaj. His father, as I've said to you, was among the dead who perished at Berisa. His body was never found, but he has never been heard from since. Of course, bearing in mind the posture of the Defence that these events never took place, you should show that there is very strong corroboration indeed of the survivors' account. First, in 2001 and 2002, the execution site was established and it soon gave up the mortal remains of nine individuals. DNA profiling, taking blood samples from family members, and testing against bone samples has confirmed that these remains belong to the individuals named in the third schedule, apart from Hetem Rexhaj, Rizah Rexhaj's father, who has never been found. This is in a sense not surprising. His son survived. The killers knew this and they may well have moved the body to another site, sensing that the surviving son might welcome back and try to recover the body. Second, upon examination of the remains by a forensic pathologist and forensic anthropologist, it was confirmed, in six instances, that the individuals perished as a result of fatal gunshot injury. In three instances the experts were either unable to establish or indeed exclude death by gunshot wounds. As I've already stated, a number of bodies demonstrated injuries consistent with having been severely beaten. Third, cartridge cases and ammunition remnants were found at the execution site, and a ballistics expert has confirmed to varying degrees of certainty that the cartridges found had been fired from an AK-47 assault weapon, the weapon used by Bala and the third guard. The origin of the ammunition was almost all from Albania itself. Evidence will be led in the case that the KLA secured much of its ammunition and logistics from Albania. Moreover, evidence will also be led from a Serb general that the Serbs did not use Albanian ammunition for a number of very good reasons, including the fact that they had plenty of their own ammunition. The murdered individuals are set out in schedule 3 of the indictment, and I will go through them -- I would have liked to have spent more time on this, but we are running out of time and I would like to finish this evening. The first victim is man by the name of Emin Emini. That is his photograph. If we could move to the next one. That is Ibush Hamza. That man is Hyzri Harjizi. This man Shaban Hoti, Your Honours, I've already mentioned him to you. He was married with two daughters and sons. As I've explained to you, he was a linguist. He spoke French and Russian. He lost his job in 1992, during a Milosevic purge of Albanians from state positions. During 1998, to make money for his family, he started using his language skills by working with foreign journalists in Kosovo. On the 26th of July, you will hear how he was accompanying three Russian journalists when they were stopped at Lapusnik, and we will bring one or two of those journalists who were present at the time who will say that they were stopped at Lapusnik. The journalists were detained for a short period of time and released. Shaban Hoti was kept by the KLA and subsequently murdered on Berisa. His family searched for him high and low after his disappearance. They even approached Fatmir Limaj about his disappearance. But the fact is his body was recovered from the group executed on Berisa by Haradin Bala. And if we could now move to the next gentleman, Hasan Hoxha. Hasan Hoxha was married with six children. He was an LDK supporter. He was kidnapped in July of 1998. Again, his family searched for him. He was directed to Petrastica, a village under Fatmir Limaj's command. While acknowledging that Hasan Hoxha was being detained by the KLA for questioning, the family, when they approached the headquarters in Petrastica were turned away and told not to come back again. The next individual is a man by the name of Safet Hysenaj. The next is a man by the name of Bashkim Rashiti. He was married with three boys and one girl. His wife believed that he was joining the KLA at Krimeravac [phoen]. She even went there to try and find him and deliver fresh clothes and see that he was all right. He has never been seen again and indeed died on the mountain at Berisa. The next gentleman is Hetem Rexhaj. That's Rizah Rexhaj's father. The next individual is Lutfi Xhemshiti. Lutfi Xhemshiti, when he was murdered, had been married for 11 years. He had four children; two boys and two girls. His wife spent months looking for him. Again, directed to the same military headquarters at Krimeravac, like Bashkim Rashiti's wife. Again, no sign of the man. And I think lastly is Shyqyri Zymeri, the last victim. If I could now, Your Honours, move to the law and evidence in respect of the responsibility of the three accused. I've mentioned some of the evidence already where it was appropriate and I would now like to develop that some more. As to the law relevant for Article 7(1) and ordering, planning, instigating or aiding and abetting, you will find that referred to in paragraphs 135 to 150 of the Prosecutor's pre-trial brief. The three accused again do not take issue with us on the law. On the mode of committing, I'll make some comments. On the other modes, I won't. It's in the pre-trial brief, and there is no dispute between the parties on the law in respect of those modes of liability. In respect of the modes of committing, we rely both on straightforward commission of the offence, where the Prosecution must prove that the accused has performed all of the elements of the actus reus of the crime and that the accused has acted with the required mens rea. So we rely on the simple form of committing, if I can call it that, physical, personal participation in the crime alleged, together with the requisite criminal intent. And of course, you can have several perpetrators for the same crime where the conduct of all satisfies the requirements of the offence. The second mode of liability, as I've already stated, under the term committing is participation by the three accused in a joint criminal enterprise. I've touched on this already. Three forms of joint criminal enterprise are alternatively pleaded in the indictment, all recognised by the jurisprudence of this institution, all legitimate vehicles to demonstrate the culpability of the three accused. The interpretation by the Appeals Chamber to include this form of liability recognises the original intention of the Security Council in establishing this court. The jurisdictional reach of this court was not to be limited only to the physical perpetrators of crimes. All who participated in serious violations of international humanitarian law would be brought to account. The concept of joint criminal enterprise logically recognises that in wartime, crimes of this nature, which you find in this indictment, are committed by groups as opposed to individuals, and acting in pursuance of a common design or purpose as opposed to an individual plan or motive. Respectfully, Your Honours, some fundamentals, if it may be of assistance to you. While it's possible for you to find that an accused aided and abetted a joint criminal enterprise, it is largely the case that an accused involved in a common purpose will be regarded as a co-perpetrator, and I believe that the evidence in this case will show that to be so. These three individuals, if they are found responsible under a joint criminal enterprise, will be found to be co-perpetrators. There are three basic requirements common to all forms of joint criminal enterprise: A plurality of persons, one; secondly, the existence of a common plan, which amounts to or involves the commission of a crime provided for in the Statute; and lastly, participation of the accused in the execution of the common design or plan. Now, the first type of joint criminal enterprise, called basic JCE, basic joint criminal enterprise, or JCE 1. Here, all the participants share a common intent, but all may be -- all may not be involved in the actual criminal act. An example would be where three men enter into a plan to imprison, beat, torture, and kill prisoners in a makeshift prison camp. While all must share the criminal intent of all of the crimes, they have different roles in the design. One may be a guard. One or two may be the torturers and the killers. Another may be the camp commander. Another, the regional commander where the camp is located and to whom the camp commander reports. But each will be liable for the parts that they play, each accountable for the contribution given. The only requirement is that they must intend the results of the plan. That is, the sum total of the crimes within the joint criminal enterprise. The second form of joint criminal enterprise, or JCE 2, as it is sometimes referred to, which is pleaded in the alternative in our indictment to the first form, is actually specifically formulated for crimes committed in camps during wartime. It requires that each of the accused have knowledge of a system of ill-treatment coupled with an intent to further that common, concerted system of ill-treatment. The 2001 Kvocka decision, a first-instance actually examined in great detail the legal development of this concept and found the case-law to demonstrate that where a detention facility was operated in such a manner that the criminal intent of the operation was patently clear, anyone who knowingly participated in any significant way in the operation of the facility or assisted or facilitated its activity incurred individual criminal responsibility for participation in the criminal enterprise, either as a co-perpetrator or as an aider and abettor, depending on the position that the individual occupied within the organisational hierarchy and the degree of that individual's participation. Now, paragraph 306 of that judgement, Your Honours, I think respectfully is helpful, and it gives a number of factors that can be used to judge the level of or degree of participation of an accused in this kind of joint criminal enterprise. Firstly, the size of the criminal enterprise; secondly, the functions performed by the accused, his position, the amount of time spent participating after acquiring knowledge of the criminality of the system, efforts made by the accused to prevent or impede the efficient functioning of the system, the seriousness and scope of the crimes committed and the efficiency, zealousness or gratuitous cruelty exhibited in performing the actor's function, direct evidence of shared intent or agreement with the criminal endeavour, such as repeated, continuous, or extensive participation in the system, verbal expressions or physical perpetration of a crime. Lastly, the role that the accused played vis-a-vis the seriousness and scope of the crimes committed. Those are factors which may assist you. It is important to stress that the culpable participant does not need to know of every crime committed within the system of ill-treatment. Knowing that these crimes are being committed, knowingly participating in that system in a way that substantially assists or facilitates the commission of a crime which allows the criminal enterprise to function effectively or efficiently is enough to establish criminal liability. Very briefly, Your Honours, the third alternative variant of the joint criminal enterprise. This is the extended form of joint criminal enterprise, where the objects and purpose of the enterprise is essentially overshot by natural and foreseeable acts of one or more of the co-perpetrators. And I think it's best demonstrated by our indictment. Here, for this form of joint criminal enterprise, the Prosecutor alleges that the object and purpose was to imprison, abuse, and torture Serb and Albanian prisoners, and that the murders alleged in counts 7 to 10, unless proven to be specifically perpetrated by one of the three accused, one or more of the three accused, that they were the natural and foreseeable consequences of the execution of the other three objectives of the plan, of the imprisonment, of the torture. That the three accused were aware that such crimes, murders were the possible outcome of the execution of the joint criminal enterprise. So if it were the case that you were to find that there was a joint criminal enterprise but that the evidence led you to find that murder, rather than being an object of the enterprise, was a natural and foreseeable consequence of the nature of the enterprise, then you could convict for this third form of joint criminal enterprise as opposed to the alternative first form that is pleaded. One last point on this form of joint criminal enterprise. At paragraphs 32 of the Musliu brief and I believe paragraph 39 of the Limaj brief, they both do not accept that this extended form of joint criminal enterprise existed in customary international law in 1998. And the two accused cite two paragraphs, 185 to 192, of the Tadic appeals judgement in support of their position. Now, the Prosecution's position is that, in fact, the Appeals Chamber in Tadic had specifically considered this form of joint criminal enterprise, at paragraph 220, and that they found that in fact it was part of customary international law in 1992. I think our position is bolstered by the fact that Tadic himself was acquitted at trial of a number of murders at first instance. He was subsequently convicted on appeal under this extended form of joint criminal enterprise. So based on appellate jurisprudence, there cannot be any suggestion that the Appeals Chamber considered that this form of joint criminal enterprise, this extended form, did not exist in 1998, as it had been specifically applied to crimes committed in 1992. Moreover, the Tadic appeals decision has recently been confirmed by the Appeals Chamber in Ojdanic, in which the Appeals Chamber was unanimous again in holding that this form of joint criminal enterprise was established in customary international law in 1992. Very briefly, the law relevant to Article 7(3) of the Statute. Only Fatmir Limaj and Isak Musliu are charged. Article 7(3) does apply to an internal armed conflict, such as the conflict which existed here. The law is set out in paragraphs 151 to 157 of the brief, of our brief. Only one issue is raised by the accused, and that is, I think, a fact which is evidential rather than legal, but I will deal with it very briefly here. Both Limaj and Musliu refer to a regrettable omission in the Prosecution brief, citing to the Appeals Chamber decision in Hadzihasanovic. That authority states that an accused may not be charged under Article 7(3) of the Statute for previous crimes committed by soldiers who subsequently fell under their command. So, in other words, where a commander inherits a soldier from another unit who has committed a crime in another unit, he can't be held responsible for those -- the commander cannot be held responsible for the crimes inherited with the soldier. On reading our indictment, honour, I think you'll find it it's clear that there was no need for the Prosecution to refer to such an authority. We do not allege that Limaj and Musliu assumed command of subordinates who had previously committed crimes. We say that they were in command of individuals who were committing crimes at the time. So that Limaj, Musliu, they were in command of soldiers who committing crimes at the time, specifically, Haradin Bala, one of the accused here. I've touched on some of the evidence linking the three accused to the criminal events charged in the indictment. I'll briefly expand on it to give you some further insight. It's not disputed, Your Honours, by the Defence that Fatmir Limaj returned from Switzerland to Kosovo in March of 1998. Fatmir Limaj confirms in an interview that while in Switzerland, he was tasked with certain business by the General Staff of the KLA. Further, it's not disputed by the Defence that he went immediately to a place called Klecka. You can see Klecka on this map. It's not marked, but I've pointed it out to you a number of times before. The Prosecutor will show that from here, he organised a regional headquarters of the KLA for the area south of the Pristina-Peja road. That area of command included many of the places where critical events referred to in the indictment took place. It was also around this time that he came to be known by the pseudonym of Celiku, or steel, the nom de guerre that I've already mentioned to you. KLA soldiers and commanders routinely adopted a nom de guerre as a personal security measure to protect their families from reprisals by Serb security forces as well as to generate legend about their exploits. In terms of Fatmir Limaj's command, I've already stated that the villages surrounding Klecka were established as what you will hear referred to as points, which were effectively KLA military concentrations. Each point consisted of a unit of KLA soldiers under a local KLA commander who was, in turn, under Fatmir Limaj's command. For example, the unit here at Lapusnik, as I've already said to you, was known as Celiku 3. Points were organised in a number of villages, including Kroimire, here, Luznica, Kisna Reka, here, Fustica, Trpeza, Javor which is not marked on -- oh, yes, Javor is marked on the map, Crnoljevo where you will recall a significant number of the victims were kidnapped, Zborce, and Rasinovac. These villages were under Fatmir Limaj's command. You will hear evidence that Fatmir Limaj regularly met with his point commanders in Klecka. So the commanders of these areas of KLA military concentration. They would report on events in their area of operations and he would issue orders. Fatmir Limaj was recognised as the commander by his subordinates. You will hear evidence from a number of sources to this effect. And his orders, Your Honours, were followed. Limaj communicated with his subordinates by messenger or courier. This is a fact confirmed and admitted to by Haradin Bala in his pre-trial brief at paragraph 13, that the KLA used couriers to communicate between units. As time went on, increasingly radio transmitters were used by the KLA to communicate between units. The position of Fatmir Limaj in his pre-trial brief is that the Prosecution grossly exaggerates the extent of the organisation, of the military organisation of the KLA during the relevant period. First, Your Honours, in order for liability to attach, as I've already stated - and it applies as much to this principle as it does to armed conflict - it's not necessary for the Prosecution to prove a level sophistication and organisation within the KLA at the relevant time which equates to a modern sophisticated army. It's fair to say that between April and July of 1998, the KLA had a rudimentary military structure which functioned. Secondly, in this case, the three accused were either constantly or, in fact, to be fair, in Limaj's case, regularly at the scene of the ongoing crimes. Fatmir Limaj paints a picture of his command authority in his pre-trial brief which, frankly, lacks credibility. He states that between March and July of 1998, he was responsible for organising men but he had no power over them; that during the period of the indictment, he was training members of the KLA, attacking Serb forces, defending Kosovar Albanian villages, but he had no de jure or de facto authority over anyone. He could encourage members of the KLA and make organisational suggestions, just like a military commander, Your Honours, but he says that he had no authority over any soldier until immediately after the end of the time period of the indictment, in August of 1998. At this stage, he's suddenly clothed with military authority. This is, in fact, when forces, existing forces under his command, were re-designated as the 121st Brigade of the KLA, so broadly the same soldiers, the same subordinates, including Isak Musliu, who actually became the deputy commander of the 121st Brigade, under Limaj, in August of 1998. The fact is, Your Honours, respectfully, you must look to the substance of matters rather than the form. Whilst there may have been some structural changes, simply because an organisation, a military organisation, changes its name from Celiku's Units to the 121st Brigade does not suddenly overnight change the existing legal and factual responsibilities and relationships between a commander and his subordinates and vice versa. Common sense dictates this. The evidence will show in this case that Fatmir Limaj did have the necessary de facto authority at least over members of the KLA in Lapusnik and other areas at the relevant time. Members of the KLA will state that Fatmir Limaj had authority and that there was a basic organisational structure. Surviving victims will say that that was their impression of matters in Lapusnik camp. Serb Security Service members will say, and independent members of the international community will say; most of all, and I will remind you what Fatmir said on the 14th of June of 1998, and I've already shown you. He didn't say it on the 14th of June - I'm sorry - but he was referring to the period of June of 1998. He was referring to the organisational structure of the KLA in June. If we could play that video again.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The KLA point, or stronghold, at Lapusnik, where the detention facility was located, was established following fighting with Serb security forces on the 9th of May of 1998. Fatmir Limaj designated this point as Celiku 3 and he placed Isak Musliu in charge. Naturally, this is disputed by the Defence. However, Mr. Musliu acknowledges in his pre-trial brief that he was the coordinator or organiser in Lapusnik but not the local commander. Mr. Bala states in his pre-trial brief that his understanding was that Mr. Musliu was the unit leader in Lapusnik from shortly after 8th May, 1998. Indeed, in Mr. Musliu's application form for the Kosovo Police Service, he states that he was employed by the KLA from 1996 and that he was in the Celiku Unit and also the 121st Brigade and that Fatmir Limaj was his commanding officer. And if we could show that document. You can see it here, an extract from Mr. Musliu's police application, where he states his employment from November 1996, Kosovo Liberation Army. First of all, Celiku Unit, becoming the 121st Brigade, based in Klecka; subsequently, commander of military police in the Nerodimlje operational zone; subsequently, coordinator for the formation of Kosovo police. Commander Fatmir Limaj. There is no qualification in that document by Mr. Musliu that between May and July of 1998, that somehow he and Mr. Limaj were colleagues of equal stature who coordinated until, suddenly, in August of 1998, he and Mr. Limaj were transformed overnight into the commander and deputy commander of the 121st Brigade. Mr. Musliu acknowledged when he was arrested that his nickname was in fact Qerqiz, and that nickname will come up a lot in this trial. As the existence of the camp itself in Lapusnik, Mr. Musliu admits in his pre-trial brief that he was present in Lapusnik, based in Lapusnik, from May to July of 1998. As I've already stated, Mr. Limaj admits in his pre-trial brief that between May and July of 1998, he visited Lapusnik, the village where the KLA detention facility which is the subject of this indictment was located, approximately 20 times. Mr. Musliu confirms in his pre-trial brief that indeed Mr. Limaj visited Lapusnik about 20 times in this period. So he corroborates his commander on this point. But both Limaj and Musliu state that there was no camp in Lapusnik, no prisoners, no beatings, no torture, and no dead attributable to them. Indeed, you will see here, on the 27th of February of 2004, when the three accused were pleading to the second amended indictment. And if we could play this short video clip. Judge Orie is reading the charges.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: "JUDGE ORIE: Count 5, which reads: 'Inhumane acts, a crime against humanity, punishable under Article 5(1), 7(1), and 7(3) of the Statute of the Tribunal.' How do you plead to count 5?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED LIMAJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We've already declared our plea even earlier, and even now we do not accept that. Let's say me personally, I do not accept that such a camp has existed, and as a result --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj, let me stop you."

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So Mr. Limaj has made it very clear that all of the events about which I am speaking to you today are complete fantasy. Let me say this, Your Honours, on behalf of the victims of the Lapusnik camp in respect of what Mr. Limaj stated at that hearing and what has been made clear by the Defence. The evidence in this case will do much more than establish that there was a camp at Lapusnik. It will also establish that Fatmir Limaj is responsible for the horrors that took place there. As I have said before, I would ask you to have this defence at the forefront of your mind throughout this trial, throughout the evidence. When you hear the Prosecutor's examination of a witness, when you hear the cross-examination by the Defence, think of this defence: no camp, no prisoners, no victims, no dead. Of course the Prosecutor's position is that this is wholly untrue, but the very nature of their defence and their admission of their presence in Lapusnik frankly leaves for no other defence. I leave it to the evidence to expose that to you. What is a fact is that from early January of 1998, a steady stream of Serbs and Albanians started to disappear across Kosovo. Many of them were taken by certain elements within the KLA. Lapusnik detention facility was a holding place for such people. Men were arrested and taken to this place over a three-month period. The kidnapping, the transportation to this central camp was coordinated and it went on for a long time it. Any civilised human being with a thread of moral conscience who entered that dreadful place in the summer of 1998 knew that the operation of the camp was patently illegal: men shackled to the floor, beaten, injured for sport, hungry, thirsty in the summer heat, stripped of all faith and feeling. Fatmir Limaj knew what was being done to the prisoners by his men. Of course he did. He was among the prisoners on his 20 visits to Lapusnik. He saw with his own eyes what I've tried to describe for you. He commanded those who brought the victims to Lapusnik. He commanded those who put the key in the lock. He commanded those who engaged in gratuitous and brutal violence. He commanded those who did the killing. He knew that this was a merciless and violent regime, and you will hear evidence that it was he who had the authority to release prisoners from Lapusnik, the power to decide on a man's fate, in many instances in this case, the power of life or death. Fatmir Limaj personally swore a number of survivors upon their release to silence on pain of death, that everything they'd experienced, everything they had suffered, would never be revealed by them. Why? To cover his guilt for these crimes. Fatmir Limaj, Commander Celiku, knew then and he knows now as he sits here before you what took place at Lapusnik during those three months because he willed it to take place. He caused it and he's legally responsible for it. Later in 1998, Fatmir Limaj admitted to members of the international community, when challenged, that the KLA was detaining civilians. In the particular instance, two Serb journalists detained by the KLA for breaching KLA regulations. These two men had been sentenced two prison terms without ever being present at their own trials. They had no access to lawyers, visits from the international community were forbidden, their location, like those at the Lapusnik camp, was a secret. The execution of the final group of ten prisoners on Berisa at the end of July 1998 was a crime in which Fatmir Limaj was not only aware of but in which I have stated to you the evidence will show he directly participated. He met the detainees and Haradin Bala as they walked to execution or release. He spoke with Bala. He issued orders. Bala released one group, the other group he marched to a clearing and with one of Limaj's soldiers and another guard, executed ten men by firing-squad, stating to them that they had been condemned to death. The KLA assured the international community, time and time again, of their commitment to the Geneva Conventions, and it's fair to say that many honourable combatants within the KLA tried hard in the face of extreme provocation to comply with international humanitarian law. But what happened at Lapusnik was a flagrant disregard of even the lowest standards of humanity. Fatmir Limaj told members of the international community that he complied with international humanitarian law, that he disciplined soldiers under his command, and you'll hear of specific examples of Limaj punishing soldiers, but you will not hear of any of the crimes that were committed in Lapusnik being investigated or punished by Limaj or anyone else. If I could just show one video clip about Fatmir Limaj's views on discipline.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So, Your Honours, Mr. Limaj was a fanatic for order and discipline. But you will not find that any of the soldiers who committed crimes at Lapusnik were disciplined, none. Indeed, you will find that Isak Musliu was promoted after the events in Lapusnik, first to Limaj's deputy within the 121st Brigade, and subsequently to commander of the military police in another operational zone of the KLA. So he was rewarded for the way that he ran Lapusnik camp, rather than punished. And with the articulated defence of the accused, no camp, no imprisonment, no torture, no dead, we do not expect any evidence whatsoever to be offered before this court of the investigation or punishment of crimes in Lapusnik. Isak Musliu, Qerqiz, commanded the soldiers at the Lapusnik point from May 1998 until July 1998. He reported directly to Fatmir Limaj. He controlled access in and out of the prison camp. He gave orders inside the camp to the soldiers. He gave orders to blindfold, to move, to beat the prisoners. As he admits himself, he was based at Lapusnik. The evidence will show that he was in the camp on a regular basis. He was an efficient and zealous commander, and there is no doubt that this man enjoyed the infliction of gratuitous and brutal violence. As I've stated already, he is a keen martial arts practitioner, and he used both these skills and various other instruments of torture to attack and terrify the prisoners. Prisoners were made to feel absolutely worthless, witnessing senseless butchery on a daily basis, believing their lives were dependent on an individual like Isak Musliu. A number of prisoners, Your Honours, were so badly beaten that their supreme desire was a speedy and painless death. I would remind Your Honours of the forensic evidence in this case, which shows a community of prisoners with absolutely appalling injuries. Isak Musliu personally participated in the murder of a number of the inmates. He ran the camp on behalf of Fatmir Limaj. And the criminal regime for which Isak Musliu was responsible for supervising is Fatmir Limaj's regime also. Musliu commanded the soldiers who operated the camp. He was in the camp from May to July of 1998. He did nothing to prevent the criminality in the camp. On the contrary; by virtue of his own murderous and brutal example, he encouraged atrocities and can be credited with repeated, continuous, extensive, and significant participation in this terrible criminal endeavour. Bearing in mind the nature of his defence, which is a mirror image of his co-accused, Fatmir Limaj, no camp, no prisoners, no torture, no dead, it hardly needs to be stated that he neither prevented nor punished any of his subordinates for the events which took place in Lapusnik. Haradin Bala, known as Shala, was a guard at Lapusnik. Musliu was his commander in the camp. It seems that there were two men known as Shala in Lapusnik. You can see the photograph of the other one here. This man, his real name is Ruzhdi Karpuzi and you can see he is physically distinct from Haradin Bala. This man had duties outside the detention facility. So when prisoners are referring to Shala being a guard in the camp, they are referring to Haradin Bala and not this man, Ruzhdi Karpuzi. In his pre-trial brief Haradin Bala confirms that Isak Musliu was the unit leader of Celiku 3, the KLA force in Lapusnik of which he, Haradin Bala, was a part. While working as a guard at Lapusnik camp, Bala work a black uniform. He had the classic role of a camp guard. He guarded the entrance to the camp, he locked and unlocked the doors of the areas of detention. On their arrival, he would take the prisoners to their cells, he would shackle the prisoners down. Bala beat the prisoners and often provided the security for others while they engaged in beatings. It was often the case that prisoners were literally tied down like animals and then blindfolded before being beaten. Bala was the one who tied and blindfolded them, preparing them for the violence to come. In this environment, he threatened the prisoners, adding to and enhancing the fear and robbing individuals of any sense of hope. The evidence that I've already referred to will show his personal involvement in a considerable number of murders in this case. I will, for completeness, mention it again, but I would remind you that on the 26th of July of 1998, it was Haradin Bala who took over 20 prisoners into the mountains above Lapusnik, to Berisa, where, on Limaj's orders, he released a number and then executed ten other prisoners. While Limaj bears responsibility for this act, Bala's culpability is straightforward on the evidence that I've outlined for you. I have already outlined the nature of his defence. It's that of a partial alibi and also now it seems within the latest 92 bis filing of the Defence, he also completely denies the existence of the camp. I'm almost completed, Your Honour. I suspect I'll be another three or four minutes. I've spent some considerable time outlining the evidence and the law in this case. That is required of me under the Rules. It is fair to say that almost all of the cases that reach the Chambers of this Tribunal concern the deeds and acts of men that we would rather not believe. That is the nature of our business. The single factor which distinguishes cases within this Tribunal is proportion: How many dead, how much torture, how much suffering, how much killing. But all cases heard within this Tribunal make daily domestic crime pale into insignificance. Here we have over 20 dead and tens of injured and many ruined lives and families. By any civilised standards, a catastrophe. We will never address every crime committed by every party in this war. That was never envisaged by the Security Council when this Tribunal was established. But never let it be said that certain groups were placed above the law by the Office of the Prosecutor. The Defence of Limaj and Musliu berate the Prosecutor in their pre-trial briefs for bringing this indictment at all, that by doing so we revise history, by suggesting that the most serious and widespread crimes in 1998 were committed by the Kosovo Liberation Army. First, Your Honours, let me make it abundantly clear that that is not what we saw at all. As I have already set out for you, the Prosecutor does not dispute that widespread human rights violations were committed during this period by Serb security forces. These violations culminated in the appalling events that have unfolded from January to June of 1999 and for which Slobodan Milosevic is currently standing trial, and for which Colonel General Pavkovic, Colonel General Lazarevic, Colonel General Djordjevic, Colonel General Lukic, Milan Milutinovic, Nikola Sainovic, Colonel General Drago Ojdanic and Vlako [phoen] Stojakovic stand accused. As to events in 1998, witnesses may give evidence before this court of Serb crimes in this period but that justifies absolutely nothing at Lapusnik. The unlawful imprisonment, torture, and murder of all of these innocent people at Lapusnik was not impelled by the needs or necessities of warfare, and the long shadow of Milosevic's crimes in Kosovo do not purge these three accused of their responsibility for what happened at Lapusnik. That is basic morality and that is the law. The foundations of this institution rest upon traditional principles of morality, justice, and the law, accumulated by civilisation over the course of the centuries. It recognises -- those principles recognise and reaffirm our faith in the dignity and worth of each of us. The acceptance that warfare is a pitiful business, but the aspiration, backed by legal compulsion, that those who are outside the combat - be they soldiers, be they civilians - should be treated with compassion and mercy. And the law recognises that these fundamental safeguards are universal, that they be applied to all victims of war, regardless of gender, ethnicity, or colour, regardless of who the perpetrators are, equal and exact justice to all men. I speak of the victims, but these words of Jefferson should be a source of great hope to the accused too. They can expect this trial to be fair. They are guaranteed all the rights and dignities which flow from the Statute of this Tribunal. They can look to the Bench of this Honourable Court as guardians of the integrity of these proceedings. They are very well defended, as they should be. As the Defence state in their pre-trial briefs, the burden, the legal burden, rests upon us, the Prosecution, to prove these appalling events and the accuseds' involvement in them. You must be satisfied of the guilt of the accused in respect of each charge beyond a reasonable doubt. That is Rule 87 and that is the golden thread, a safeguard which all three accused must enjoy. I will not expand on what it means. In my home jurisdiction, such explanation often causes problems for judges and counsel alike. As it is, you are professional Judges. I do not need to explain to you what it means. You know much better than I what it means. You are finders of fact and law. It only needs for me to say that the Prosecution will discharge the legal burden in this case. Kosovo today is a partitioned society. Long years of repression and division, and this most recent war, Your Honours, has left very deep scars indeed. People are grieving, angry, and bitter on both sides of the ethnic divide. But in this indictment you will find Serb victims and you will find Albanian victims. The sons and fathers of both communities, a common sorrow, a shared anguish which could be a bridge of reconciliation between the two communities. After all, one of the principal purposes for which this institution was established by its founding fathers was to try and create reconciliation within the region. So a belief once again amongst these people that their neighbours are indeed like them. What men do in warfare for good or ill lasts a relatively brief period, but it is those acts which affect the whole character of the peace which lasts a much longer period. Unless the criminal acts of warfare are honestly and openly addressed, however difficult that may be, they leave a bitter and violent legacy. The capacity and willingness of a people to confront the terrible crimes of a very few amongst them is a sure sign of national maturity and progress. Sylejman Selimi, a Kosovar Albanian and highly respected military commander in Kosovo today said this about war crimes generally: "Every democratic country should come to terms with people who committed crimes during war, even countries that have perfected the system, the democratic systems still have problems, let alone us starting out without any experience. And of course there is no one above the law. People may do things in the euphoria of the moment and then afterwards they have to take responsibility." Your Honours, I'm complete. I must now let the evidence speak. In closing, I would only say to you it is my firm and honest belief that if the evidence in this case is freely and fairly heard it will prove these men for what they are, murderers and torturers. That is what the Prosecutor asserts. That is what the evidence will show, and that, most respectfully, Your Honours, is what the law will require you to find in this case. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cayley, for that careful opening. As counsel will have noted, because of the need for this trial to be translated into a fourth language, and therefore the need for additional space for interpreters, we have very limited facilities in which to conduct this trial and must share this courtroom with another trial that is being conducted. The inconvenience of that to all is regretted, but it is a reality we all have to deal with. In immediate effect is that we will continue tomorrow morning at 9.00, to finish by 1.45, because the courtroom is needed in the afternoon for other purposes. But at present we expect for the remainder of the week to continue in the afternoon session, that is, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, 2.15 for 7.00 in the evening. So we will now adjourn until tomorrow morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 16th day of November, 2004, at 9.00 a.m.
